subsections.subtitle: The Liturgy is the summit toward which the activity of the Church is directed, and at the same time the font from which all her power flows.

content.value:
The Liturgy, "through which the work of our redemption is accomplished," most of all in the divine sacrifice of the Eucharist, is the outstanding means whereby the faithful may express in their lives, and manifest to others, the mystery of Christ and the real nature of the true Church.

It is of the essence of the Church that she be both human and divine, visible and yet invisibly equipped, eager to act and yet intent on contemplation, present in this world and yet not at home in it; and she is all these things in such wise that in her the human is directed and subordinated to the divine, the visible likewise to the invisible, action to contemplation, and this present world to that city yet to come, which we seek

![img:img-4499.jpg|left|w:50%|Paolo Veronese - Baptism of Christ]
To accomplish so great a work, Christ is always present in his Church, especially in her liturgical celebrations. He is present in the sacrifice of the Mass, not only in the person of his minister, "the same now offering, through the ministry of priests, who formerly offered himself on the cross," but especially under the Eucharistic species. By his power he is present in the sacraments, so that when someone baptizes it is really Christ himself who baptizes. He is present in his word, since it is he himself who speaks when Sacred Scripture is read in the Church. He is present, lastly, when the Church prays and sings psalms, the same who promised: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20).

Indeed, in this great work by which God is perfectly glorified and men are sanctified, Christ always associates with himself his most beloved Bride, the Church, who calls upon her Lord and through him offers worship to the Eternal Father

@@The Liturgy (from the ecclesiastical Latin _liturgīa_, itself from the Greek _leitourguía_, meaning "public service" or "work on behalf of the people") includes the Mass, all the sacraments, the Liturgy of the Hours, blessings, rites, and any liturgical act, such as, for example, the Liturgy of the Word or the Good Friday liturgy (which are not Masses, because there is no consecration).@@

subsections.subtitle: If the angels could envy anything, they would envy the Holy Mass. —St. Pius X
keyPoints: Why Take Part in the Mass?

content.value:
The Mass is, at one and the same time and inseparably, the sacrificial memorial in which the sacrifice of the cross is perpetuated, and the sacred banquet of communion in the Body and Blood of the Lord. But the celebration of the eucharistic sacrifice is wholly ordered toward the intimate union of the faithful with Christ through communion. To receive Communion is to receive Christ himself, who offers himself for us.

In the Mass, Christ is present in a special way:

- In his Word, because he himself speaks when the Scriptures are read
- In the sacrifice, through the ministry of the Church
- And especially under the eucharistic species
- When the Church prays and sings psalms

Finally, the Mass does not end at the altar: it concludes with the sending forth (missio), so that the faithful may fulfill God's will in their daily life. Thus the Mass is memory that saves, communion that transforms, and mission that enlightens the world.
In this divine sacrifice which is offered in the Mass, that same Christ is contained and offered in an unbloody manner who once offered himself in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross.
content.author: Council of Trent

content.value: Why Take Part in the Mass?
The Eucharist is the compendium and sum of our faith.
content.author: St. Thomas Aquinas

content.value:
Among all the liturgical actions, Holy Mass occupies an eminent and central place. Just as the liturgy is the summit and source of the whole Christian life, so Holy Mass is the summit and source of the whole liturgy. Jesus Christ instituted this sacrament at the Last Supper. The first Christian community never failed to gather to fulfill the Lord's command: «Do this in remembrance of me».

«For this reason the faithful are obliged to participate in the Eucharist on days of obligation, unless [[excused|excusados]] for a serious reason (for example, illness, the care of infants) or dispensed by their own pastor. Those who deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin.». (_CCC_ 2181)

![img:La-ultima-cena-pintura.jpg|left|w:50%|Last Supper by Pietro Lorenzetti]
However, we should not attend the Eucharist merely out of obligation or fear of sin, but rather moved by love of God above all things; by our need to repent and ask forgiveness for our sins; by our need to hear his Word, which is light and food for our life; to thank him for all he gives us undeservedly throughout the week and throughout our lives; to unite ourselves to the sacrifice of Christ on the cross so that we may one day also share in his glorious resurrection; to be nourished by the Body and Blood of Christ so as to have strength and not succumb to temptation; to meet our brothers and sisters who share the same faith as we do and together praise God, give him glory, adore him, sing to him, and offer our petitions for the whole Church and for the entire world.

content.value:
The purpose of the Introductory Rites is to constitute the Church-Assembly, gather it together, and prepare it to receive the Word of God in a spirit of prayer and with sufficient openness to conversion.

The Introductory Rites bring the assembly into the celebration and prepare it to take an active part in the two principal parts of the Holy Mass: the **Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist**. And, as the fruit of this participation, to obtain all the graces the Lord pours out upon his gathered people.

That is why it is important to arrive with time to spare and to enter in silence and attentiveness: this is how the assembly truly begins to pray and to dispose itself interiorly from the very start.

The entrance procession is like saying: "We set out on the way toward God." It is not merely a movement from one place to another, but the beginning of the celebration: the chant opens the Mass, interiorly unites those gathered, and directs everyone's minds to the mystery about to be celebrated, as we accompany the priest and ministers on their way to the altar.

This is the first of the five processions found in the Holy Mass. The others are: the procession with the Book of the Gospels from the altar to the ambo, the procession of gifts, the Communion procession, and the closing procession.

Processing reminds us of our condition as pilgrims in the world. We walk through life with a clearly defined destination: the House of God the Father, our eternal home.
The entrance procession is the visible beginning of our worship: as we enter toward the altar, the chant unites our assembly and directs us to the mystery we are celebrating.
content.author: Cf. GIRM 47

content.value:
It is the assembly's first expression of prayer: it manifests faith, fosters unity, introduces the mystery of the celebration, and expresses the joy of God's children as they gather around the Lord.

It should have a processional character — that is, it should speak of walking, of pilgrimage, of ascending, of journeying together as Church, in unity; of moving toward the Father's house, of arriving at the altar, of setting out, of advancing, of rising up and pressing on. It should carry a touch of enthusiasm, energy, and joy to enliven the assembly.

For the prayers, the text must be respected exactly as it appears in the Roman Missal

When they reach the [[sanctuary|presbiterio]], the priest, the [[deacon|Diácono]], and the ministers reverence the altar with a profound bow. If the [[tabernacle|Sagrario]] is located in the sanctuary area, a genuflection should be made beforehand. The concelebrating priests, the presider (the priest who presides), and the deacon kiss the altar as a greeting of veneration to Christ, since it is his presence.

![img:Guadalupe-Incienso.jpg|left|w:50%]
The thurifer immediately comes forward with the boat so that the presider may put incense in the thurible and begin to incense the altar, the crucifix, and the image of the patron saint. When the incensing begins, a bow is made, since everything that is incensed is a symbolic and sacramental presence of Christ.

Incense in the liturgy symbolizes our prayers rising into God's presence; it is the sweet and pleasing fragrance of Christ present in the liturgy; it is an offering to the divinity and holiness of God; it is profound veneration of everything that signifies the presence of Christ: the Assembly, the Altar, the Word, the Eucharistic Gifts, the Priest.

Once the incensation is finished, the one presiding the celebration goes immediately to the chair, from where, in the name of the Lord, he will preside over the celebrating assembly.

There may be a discreet stand on which to place the [[Missal|Misal Romano]] Roman or the [[Ordinary|Ordinario]] of the Mass, and the Introductory Rites begin.

At this point the intentions for which the Holy Mass is being offered may be read. If there was no entrance chant, this is the moment to recite the entrance antiphon.

![img:catholic-church-england-and-wales36.jpg|right|w:50%]
The initial greeting is the dialogue that takes place after the Sign of the Cross. Through this greeting, the priest declares to the assembly that the Lord is present; and, with the people's response, **the mystery of the Church gathered together is made manifest.**

Example:
**Priest:** _The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all._
**People:** _And with your spirit._

This is the first of the four liturgical greetings found in the Holy Mass. The others are: before the proclamation of the Gospel, at the beginning of the Eucharistic Prayer, and before the final blessing.

These are brief interventions or explanations of a pedagogical and pastoral character given during the celebration of the Holy Mass — for example, at the beginning, before the readings, and so on. Their purpose is to prepare, guide, and introduce the faithful into the liturgical mystery, helping them to achieve an interior, active, conscious, and fruitful participation in the different moments of the Holy Sacrifice.

These commentaries should be carefully prepared, with clear sobriety. In the exercise of this ministry, the commentator stands in a suitable place facing the faithful, **but not at the ambo.**

The Act of Penitence opens the Mass by disposing the community to recognize its condition as sinners and to ask for God's mercy. The Holy Spirit moves us to conversion and repentance.

In this common prayer, the desire for reconciliation is expressed; the priest concludes the rite with an absolution that prepares us, but does not have the efficacy of the Sacrament of Penance (confession).

The Act of Penitence allows us to take part in the Holy Mass with a heart that is cleaner and more disposed to forgiveness.

After the greeting and the commentary, the priest invites those present to the Act of Penitence, which, after a brief moment of silence, the whole community carries out using one of the three existing formulas that the priest may choose.

content.title: Formulas of the Act of Penitence

tabs.label: Formula 1
tabs.value:
This is a formula based on a public confession of sins, in a general rather than particular way: _"I confess to almighty God and to you, my brothers and sisters, that I have greatly sinned, in my thoughts..."_

Besides the public confession, the penitent asks for heavenly and earthly intercession: _"therefore I ask blessed Mary ever-Virgin, all the Angels and Saints, and you, my brothers and sisters, to pray for me to the Lord our God..."_

This is a beautiful penitential formula that helps us always and humbly acknowledge our condition as sinners, against the contemporary notion held by some Christians that nothing is a sin anymore, or that they are free of all guilt.

It also fosters the attitude Christians should always have of praying for one another, of interceding for others, especially in moments when they have had the misfortune of falling into sin. It is the solidarity in prayer that we should have with one another. This Formula 1 is especially recommended for use during the Church's preparatory and penitential seasons: Advent and Lent.

The formula ends with an absolution from the priest: _"May almighty God have mercy on us, forgive us our sins..."_ This absolution, accompanied by our sincere repentance, has an effect on so-called venial or light sins, never on grave or mortal sins. For the forgiveness of these, it is necessary to approach the Sacrament of Reconciliation.

tabs.label: Formula 2
tabs.value:
This is a public acknowledgment that God is merciful. But to obtain that mercy from God, we ourselves must acknowledge our limitations and our condition as sinners; otherwise, we cannot obtain mercy.

It is based on a twofold petition for mercy from the presider: _"have mercy"_ and _"show us"_ mercy. The assembly, for its part, acknowledges its sinfulness: _"for we have sinned against you"_. And it affirms that only God's mercy can grant us salvation: _"and grant us your salvation"_. This Formula 2 is recommended for use throughout Ordinary Time. Like Formula 1, it concludes with an absolution from the priest that has the same effects already explained above.

tabs.label: Formula 3
tabs.value:
These are invocations perfectly suited to each liturgical season, addressed to Christ, that highlight some theological aspect of him and make anamnesis (remembrance) of his saving work. Each invocation ends with either _"Lord, have mercy or Christ, have mercy"_ as the case may be. Therefore, the choir or those responsible for the singing should omit the "Lord, have mercy" or "Kyrie eleison." The priest makes the invocation, adding _"Lord, have mercy"_, and the people respond by repeating _"Lord, have mercy."_

It is recommended to use this formula especially during the strong seasons of Christmas and Easter, on Sundays in Ordinary Time, and on feasts. But like the previous formulas, it is one we may use always and at any time.

content.title: Sacramentals in Place of the Act of Penitence
content.text:
**Rite of Blessing**
On Sundays, especially during the Easter Season, the blessing and sprinkling of water in memory of Baptism may be done in place of the Act of Penitence.

Sunday is the paschal day par excellence, and Baptism is the sacrament through which we are brought into Christ's Paschal Mystery. For this reason, the blessing and sprinkling with holy water is recommended on Sundays, and especially on the Sundays of the Easter Season, as a remembrance of our baptism. Holy water is not something magical, meant to "cleanse" or to "ward off evil spirits." The blessing with holy water is a sacramental.

**The Imposition of Ashes**
Another sacramental that leads us to omit the Act of Penitence is the imposition of ashes on the Wednesday that opens the season of Lent, which is fittingly called "Ash Wednesday."

One of the formulas used for the imposition of ashes says: _"Repent, and believe in the Gospel."_ Repentance is one of the necessary conditions for receiving absolution in the Sacrament of Reconciliation. If, as the ashes are imposed on us, we are invited to repent, we are being indirectly invited to approach the Sacrament of Reconciliation. We could just as well say: _"Confess, and believe in the Gospel."_

**Blessing of Candles (Presentation of the Lord / Candlemas)**
Here the priest blesses the candles the faithful hold in their hands; they are lit, and the procession begins. The priest arrives at the altar, makes the due reverence and greeting, and goes to the chair to intone the Gloria.

As we can see, the Act of Penitence is omitted. In its place is the blessing of the candles, which recall the candle of our baptism and symbolize Christ the Light.

This sacramental reminds us that we must not live in the darkness of sin, because we are children of the light who have been illumined by Christ since the day of our baptism. That symbolic light I carry in my hand invites me to approach the Sacrament of Reconciliation so as not to live in the darkness of sin. We can clearly see how the sacramental itself leads me to the sacrament.

**Blessing of Palms (Palm Sunday)**
On this day we commemorate Christ's entry into the holy city of Jerusalem to consummate his Paschal Mystery. The celebration of Mass begins in a place other than the church. After greeting the people, the priest blesses the palm branches the faithful hold in their hands. The Gospel is then proclaimed, and the procession begins. On arriving at the altar, the priest makes the due reverence and goes to the chair for the collect.

As we can see, the Act of Penitence is omitted. In its place are the blessing of the palms, the Gospel, and the procession. Processing with palms signifies Christ's paschal victory, the definitive victory over sin. This sacramental, joined to an act of popular piety, therefore also invites us to fight against sin in order to attain the palm of eternal victory.

In this daily struggle we must constantly turn to the Sacrament of Reconciliation, which heals the wounds of sin and restores us to health.

**NOTE:**
- The Act of Penitence is also omitted during the Easter Vigil, at the blessing of the new fire and the paschal candle.
- When Baptism and Marriage are celebrated within the Mass.
- When the Liturgy of the Hours is joined to the Mass, with the psalmody taking the place of the Act of Penitence.
- At the dedication of churches and altars.

content.value:
After the Act of Penitence, the invocations _"Lord, have mercy"_ (_Kyrie eleison_) follow, unless Formula 3 was used, which already includes them.

It is a chant in which the faithful acclaim Christ as "Lord" and ask for mercy (invoking: Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy).

It is the only chant in Greek that the Latin liturgy has preserved, underscoring the Eastern sense of "exomologesis" — that is, the confession and proclamation of the lordship of the risen Christ over humanity and its history.

The Gloria is a most ancient and venerable hymn with which the Church, gathered in the Holy Spirit, glorifies God the Father and glorifies and entreats the Lamb. It is, above all, a Trinitarian invocation, a beautiful doxology or praise of God, whose principal source is Sacred Scripture, but also the poetic inspiration of the early Christian communities.

The text of this hymn may not be replaced by any other. It is intoned by the priest or, depending on the circumstances, by the cantor or the choir; it is then sung by everyone together, or by the people alternating with the cantors, or by the cantors alone. If it is not sung, it is recited aloud by everyone together, or by two choirs responding to one another.

It is sung or said aloud on Sundays outside the Seasons of Advent and Lent, on solemnities and feasts, and on certain particularly solemn celebrations.

The three celebrations of the liturgical year on which the Gloria should have a more solemn and festive character are: Christmas night, the Mass _in cena Domini_, and the Easter Vigil.

This is the prayer with which the Introductory Rites of the Holy Mass conclude, just before the Liturgy of the Word begins.

When the Gloria has ended, the presider invites the assembly to pray, and everyone, together with the priest, keeps a moment of silence to become aware of being in God's presence and to formulate their petitions interiorly. The priest then, extending his hands, says the prayer usually called the "collect," which expresses the character of the celebration.

By an ancient tradition of the Church, the collect is ordinarily addressed to God the Father, through Christ, in the Holy Spirit, and concludes with the trinitarian ending — that is, the longer ending — in this way:

**If addressed to the Father:**

`"Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever."`

**Example: The Chair of Saint Peter, Apostle:**

`"Grant, we pray, almighty God, that no tempests may disturb us, for you have set us fast on the rock of the Apostle Peter's confession of faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever."`


**If addressed to the Father, but the Son is mentioned at the end:**

`"Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever."`


**If addressed to the Son:**

`"Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever."`


The people, joining in the petition, make the prayer their own with the acclamation Amen.

This prayer is one of the three prayers in the Mass called "presidential," because only the one presiding the celebration may say it. The other two presidential prayers are: the prayer over the offerings and the prayer after Communion.

subsections.subtitle: God himself speaks to his people
keyPoints: Acclamation Before the Gospel (We Speak to God)

content.value:
**We are nourished at the table of the Word of God.**

![img:frlawrence-sanvitalemoses.jpg|left|w:50%]
The Liturgy of the Word is a true dialogue: when God speaks, we listen; and when we speak, God listens to us.

It is Christ himself who speaks to us when Sacred Scripture is proclaimed in the liturgy. We must listen to him, for he is the Beloved of the Father; we must sit joyfully at his feet to hear his divine Word, for we are certain that Christ alone has the words of eternal life.

**In this context, the [[ambo|ambón]] is the place where the readings are proclaimed and one of the places where the homily should be given (the other is the chair).**

content.title: On God's Revelation in Sacred Scripture
content.text: In His goodness and wisdom God chose to reveal Himself and to make known to us the hidden purpose of His will (see Eph. 1:9) by which through Christ, the Word made flesh, man might in the Holy Spirit have access to the Father and come to share in the divine nature (see Eph. 2:18; 2 Peter 1:4). Through this revelation, therefore, the invisible God (see Col. 1;15, 1 Tim. 1:17) out of the abundance of His love speaks to men as friends (see Ex. 33:11; John 15:14-15) and lives among them (see Bar. 3:38), so that He may invite and take them into fellowship with Himself. This plan of revelation is realized by deeds and words having an inner unity: the deeds wrought by God in the history of salvation manifest and confirm the teaching and realities signified by the words, while the words proclaim the deeds and clarify the mystery contained in them. By this revelation then, the deepest truth about God and the salvation of man shines out for our sake in Christ, who is both the mediator and the fullness of all revelation

tabs.label: REVELATION ITSELF
tabs.value:
**The Nature and Object of Revelation**

2. In His goodness and wisdom God chose to reveal Himself and to make known to us the hidden purpose of His will (see Eph. 1:9) by which through Christ, the Word made flesh, man might in the Holy Spirit have access to the Father and come to share in the divine nature (see Eph. 2:18; 2 Peter 1:4). Through this revelation, therefore, the invisible God (see Col. 1;15, 1 Tim. 1:17) out of the abundance of His love speaks to men as friends (see Ex. 33:11; John 15:14-15) and lives among them (see Bar. 3:38), so that He may invite and take them into fellowship with Himself. This plan of revelation is realized by deeds and words having an inner unity: the deeds wrought by God in the history of salvation manifest and confirm the teaching and realities signified by the words, while the words proclaim the deeds and clarify the mystery contained in them. By this revelation then, the deepest truth about God and the salvation of man shines out for our sake in Christ, who is both the mediator and the fullness of all revelation.

**The Preparation for the Gospel Revelation**

3. God, who through the Word creates all things (see John 1:3) and keeps them in existence, gives men an enduring witness to Himself in created realities (see Rom. 1:19-20). Planning to make known the way of heavenly salvation, He went further and from the start manifested Himself to our first parents. Then after their fall His promise of redemption aroused in them the hope of being saved (see Gen. 3:15) and from that time on He ceaselessly kept the human race in His care, to give eternal life to those who perseveringly do good in search of salvation (see Rom. 2:6-7). Then, at the time He had appointed He called Abraham in order to make of him a great nation (see Gen. 12:2). Through the patriarchs, and after them through Moses and the prophets, He taught this people to acknowledge Himself the one living and true God, provident father and just judge, and to wait for the Savior promised by Him, and in this manner prepared the way for the Gospel down through the centuries.

**Revelation Reaches Its Fulfillment in Christ**

4. Then, after speaking in many and varied ways through the prophets, "now at last in these days God has spoken to us in His Son" (Heb. 1:1-2). For He sent His Son, the eternal Word, who enlightens all men, so that He might dwell among men and tell them of the innermost being of God (see John 1:1-18). Jesus Christ, therefore, the Word made flesh, was sent as "a man to men." He "speaks the words of God" (John 3;34), and completes the work of salvation which His Father gave Him to do (see John 5:36; John 17:4). To see Jesus is to see His Father (John 14:9). For this reason Jesus perfected revelation by fulfilling it through his whole work of making Himself present and manifesting Himself: through His words and deeds, His signs and wonders, but especially through His death and glorious resurrection from the dead and final sending of the Spirit of truth. Moreover He confirmed with divine testimony what revelation proclaimed, that God is with us to free us from the darkness of sin and death, and to raise us up to life eternal. The Christian dispensation, therefore, as the new and definitive covenant, will never pass away and we now await no further new public revelation before the glorious manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ (see 1 Tim. 6:14 and Tit. 2:13).

_DOGMATIC CONSTITUTION DEI VERBUM ON DIVINE REVELATION_

tabs.label: HANDING ON DIVINE REVELATION
tabs.value:
7. In His gracious goodness, God has seen to it that what He had revealed for the salvation of all nations would abide perpetually in its full integrity and be handed on to all generations. Therefore Christ the Lord in whom the full revelation of the supreme God is brought to completion (see 2 Cor. 1:20; 3:13; 4:6), commissioned the Apostles to preach to all men that Gospel which is the source of all saving truth and moral teaching, and to impart to them heavenly gifts. This Gospel had been promised in former times through the prophets, and Christ Himself had fulfilled it and promulgated it with His lips. This commission was faithfully fulfilled by the Apostles who, by their oral preaching, by example, and by observances handed on what they had received from the lips of Christ, from living with Him, and from what He did, or what they had learned through the prompting of the Holy Spirit. The commission was fulfilled, too, by those Apostles and apostolic men who under the inspiration of the same Holy Spirit committed the message of salvation to writing.

But in order to keep the Gospel forever whole and alive within the Church, the Apostles left bishops as their successors, "handing over" to them "the authority to teach in their own place." This sacred tradition, therefore, and Sacred Scripture of both the Old and New Testaments are like a mirror in which the pilgrim Church on earth looks at God, from whom she has received everything, until she is brought finally to see Him as He is, face to face (see 1 John 3:2).

_DOGMATIC CONSTITUTION DEI VERBUM ON DIVINE REVELATION_

tabs.label: THE OLD TESTAMENT
tabs.value:
**The History of Salvation Recorded in the Books of the Old Testament**

14. In carefully planning and preparing the salvation of the whole human race the God of infinite love, by a special dispensation, chose for Himself a people to whom He would entrust His promises. First He entered into a covenant with Abraham (see Gen. 15:18) and, through Moses, with the people of Israel (see Ex. 24:8). To this people which He had acquired for Himself, He so manifested Himself through words and deeds as the one true and living God that Israel came to know by experience the ways of God with men. Then too, when God Himself spoke to them through the mouth of the prophets, Israel daily gained a deeper and clearer understanding of His ways and made them more widely known among the nations (see Ps. 21:29; 95:1-3; Is. 2:1-5; Jer. 3:17). The plan of salvation foretold by the sacred authors, recounted and explained by them, is found as the true word of God in the books of the Old Testament: these books, therefore, written under divine inspiration, remain permanently valuable. "For all that was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope" (Rom. 15:4).

**The Importance of the Old Testament for Christians**

15. The principal purpose to which the plan of the old covenant was directed was to prepare for the coming of Christ, the redeemer of all and of the messianic kingdom, to announce this coming by prophecy (see Luke 24:44; John 5:39; 1 Peter 1:10), and to indicate its meaning through various types (see 1 Cor. 10:12). Now the books of the Old Testament, in accordance with the state of mankind before the time of salvation established by Christ, reveal to all men the knowledge of God and of man and the ways in which God, just and merciful, deals with men. These books, though they also contain some things which are incomplete and temporary, nevertheless show us true divine pedagogy. These same books, then, give expression to a lively sense of God, contain a store of sublime teachings about God, sound wisdom about human life, and a wonderful treasury of prayers, and in them the mystery of our salvation is present in a hidden way. Christians should receive them with reverence.

**The Unity of Both Testaments**

16. God, the inspirer and author of both Testaments, wisely arranged that the New Testament be hidden in the Old and the Old be made manifest in the New. For, though Christ established the new covenant in His blood (see Luke 22:20; 1 Cor. 11:25), still the books of the Old Testament with all their parts, caught up into the proclamation of the Gospel, acquire and show forth their full meaning in the New Testament (see Matt. 5:17; Luke 24:27; Rom. 16:25-26; 2 Cor. 14:16) and in turn shed light on it and explain it.

_DOGMATIC CONSTITUTION DEI VERBUM ON DIVINE REVELATION_

tabs.label: THE NEW TESTAMENT
tabs.value:
**The Excellence of the New Testament**

17. The word of God, which is the power of God for the salvation of all who believe (see Rom. 1:16), is set forth and shows its power in a most excellent way in the writings of the New Testament. For when the fullness of time arrived (see Gal. 4:4), the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us in His fullness of graces and truth (see John 1:14). Christ established the kingdom of God on earth, manifested His Father and Himself by deeds and words, and completed His work by His death, resurrection and glorious Ascension and by the sending of the Holy Spirit. Having been lifted up from the earth, He draws all men to Himself (see John 12:32, Greek text), He who alone has the words of eternal life (see John 6:68). This mystery had not been manifested to other generations as it was now revealed to His holy Apostles and prophets in the Holy Spirit (see Eph. 3:4-6, Greek text), so that they might preach the Gospel, stir up faith in Jesus, Christ and Lord, and gather together the Church. Now the writings of the New Testament stand as a perpetual and divine witness to these realities.

**The Apostolic Origin of the Gospels**

18. It is common knowledge that among all the Scriptures, even those of the New Testament, the Gospels have a special preeminence, and rightly so, for they are the principal witness for the life and teaching of the incarnate Word, our savior. The Church has always and everywhere held and continues to hold that the four Gospels are of apostolic origin. For what the Apostles preached in fulfillment of the commission of Christ, afterwards they themselves and apostolic men, under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, handed on to us in writing: the foundation of faith, namely, the fourfold Gospel, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

**The Historical Character of the Gospels**

19. Holy Mother Church has firmly and with absolute constancy held, and continues to hold, that the four Gospels just named, whose historical character the Church unhesitatingly asserts, faithfully hand on what Jesus Christ, while living among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation until the day He was taken up into heaven (see Acts 1:1). Indeed, after the Ascension of the Lord the Apostles handed on to their hearers what He had said and done. This they did with that clearer understanding which they enjoyed after they had been instructed by the glorious events of Christ's life and taught by the light of the Spirit of truth. The sacred authors wrote the four Gospels, selecting some things from the many which had been handed on by word of mouth or in writing, reducing some of them to a synthesis, explaining some things in view of the situation of their churches and preserving the form of proclamation but always in such fashion that they told us the honest truth about Jesus. For their intention in writing was that either from their own memory and recollections, or from the witness of those who "themselves from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word" we might know "the truth" concerning those matters about which we have been instructed (see Luke 1:2-4).

**The Remaining Writings of the New Testament**

20. Besides the four Gospels, the canon of the New Testament also contains the epistles of St. Paul and other apostolic writings, composed under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, by which, according to the wise plan of God, those matters which concern Christ the Lord are confirmed, His true teaching is more and more fully stated, the saving power of the divine work of Christ is preached, the story is told of the beginnings of the Church and its marvelous growth, and its glorious fulfillment is foretold. For the Lord Jesus was with His apostles as He had promised (see Matt. 28:20) and sent them the advocate Spirit who would lead them into the fullness of truth (see John 16:13).

_DOGMATIC CONSTITUTION DEI VERBUM ON DIVINE REVELATION_

content.value: For in the readings, as explained by the homily, God speaks to his people, opening up to them the mystery of redemption and salvation, and offering them spiritual nourishment; and Christ himself is present in the midst of the faithful through his word. By their silence and singing the people make God’s word their own, and they also affirm their adherence to it by means of the Profession of Faith. Finally, having been nourished by it, they pour out their petitions in the Prayer of the Faithful for the needs of the entire Church and for the salvation of the whole world.
content.author: GIRM 55

content.value:
If there is an introductory remark, the commentator gives it at this point, helping to prepare the assembly for attentive listening and introducing this important moment of the celebration. The introduction should not be lengthy, nor should it discuss the themes of each reading.

The commentator should speak only once, at the beginning of the entire Liturgy of the Word, with a brief and clear introduction. The commentator should never seek the spotlight, since what matters is not the introduction but the Word of God that is about to be proclaimed.

The First Reading introduces the faithful to the history of Salvation. It is usually taken from the Old Testament to reveal God's promises that will be fulfilled in Christ. During the Easter Season, however —from the Resurrection to Pentecost— this reading is taken from the Acts of the Apostles, giving vivid testimony to the origins, the power of the Holy Spirit, and the growth of the first ecclesial community.

For [[Ordinary Time|Tiempo Ordinario]], on the weekday Masses from Monday to Saturday, a two-year cycle of readings is followed, for odd- and even-numbered years.

A distinctive feature of the Word of God is its operative dynamism. The Word of God is not limited to conveying knowledge and messages; above all, it is actio Dei, a movement that does not return empty without having accomplished that for which it was spoken (Is 55, 11).

content.title: Recommendations
content.value: Pay attention to the readings by looking at the lector. Save the parish bulletin for reading at home or before Mass.

It is a song taken from the Psalter, chosen for its theme and linked to the reading just proclaimed, «enabling God's word to enter more deeply into the mind and heart of the one listening or reading.» (_General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours, GILH_ 172), «whose text has been drawn from traditional sources or freshly composed, in order to throw new light on the passage just read, put it in the context of the history of salvation, lead from the Old Testament to the New, turn what has been read into prayer and contemplation, or provide pleasant variety by its poetic beauty.» (GILH 169). 

![img:gerard-van-honthorst-king-david-playing-the-harp.jpg|right|w:50%|Honthorst, David Playing the Harp]
The psalms are not merely poetic texts: they are prayer. In the Christian tradition, the Psalms are the “teacher” of prayer and form an essential, enduring element of the Church's prayer, suited to every condition and season, both personal and communal.

The psalm helps us interiorize the Word of God. Through it we respond with praise, committing ourselves to the God who speaks to us.

The divine Word has many facets: it creates, liberates, saves, reconciles, calls together (convocatio), and gathers (congregatio). The convocatio underscores God's initiative and the fact that the assembly gathers because it has been called together by him. The congregatio refers rather to man's response: having been called, he gathers.

The Second Reading is the proclamation of the apostolic writings —taken from the Epistles or the Book of Revelation— which is reserved exclusively for [[Sundays, Solemnities, and Feasts|domingos, solemnidades y fiestas]]. Through it, the apostles offer the community pastoral and spiritual guidance for living out Christ's teaching in daily life and in the Church's journey.

«the word of reconciliation (2 Cor 5, 19) effects reconciliation. The word of salvation (Acts 13, 26) effects salvation. The word of grace (Acts 14, 3, 20, 32) bestows grace. The word of life (Phil 2, 16; Heb 4, 12; 1 Pet 1, 23) communicates life».
content.author: Yves Congar

It is a poetic composition that helps us better understand the mystery being celebrated. Once very numerous, today only four remain:

Two obligatory sequences: Easter and Pentecost.
Two optional sequences: the Body and Blood of Christ, and Our Lady of Sorrows.

content.title: Corpus Christi Sequence
content.text:
Let us praise the Savior, who is our shepherd and guide.
Let us praise him with hymns and songs of joy.
Let us praise him without limit and with all our strength;
for so great is the Lord that our praise falls short.

Gladly today we acclaim Christ, who is our bread,
for he is the bread of life, who gives us immortal life.
Twelve were they who dined, and he gave bread to the twelve.
Twelve then ate of it, and afterward, all mankind.

Let our praise be full and filled with joyful song;
let our soul overflow in one whole sacred harmony.
Today we celebrate with joy the glorious institution
of this divine banquet, the banquet of the Lord.

This is the new Passover, the Passover of the one King,
which brings to an end the heavy covenant of the law.
This new thing, ever new, is the light of truth,
which replaces the old with fresh clarity.

At that last supper Christ worked the wonder
of leaving his friends the memorial of his life.
Taught by the Church, we consecrate bread and wine,
which redeem us and give us strength along the way.

It is a dogma of the Christian that the bread becomes flesh,
and what was wine before is turned into blood.
There are things we do not understand, for reason cannot grasp them;
but if we see them with faith, they will enter the heart.

Under different symbols and various figures
are hidden certain wonderful, profound truths.
His Blood is our drink; his Flesh, our food;
yet in the bread or in the wine, Christ is wholly present.

Whoever eats him does not break him, does not part or divide him;
he is the whole and the part; he lives in whoever receives him.
Only one person may come forward to the altar,
or there may be multitudes: Christ will never be spent.

The good and the wicked eat him, to different effect;
it is not the same to have life as to be condemned to death.
To the wicked he brings death, and to the good he brings life.
How different an effect the very same food can have!

If they break it, do not worry; they break only what is outward;
in the smallest fragment the whole Lord is present.
When they break what is outward, they break only what you have seen;
it is no diminishment of the person of Christ.

The bread that comes down from heaven is food for travelers.
It is bread for the children. It must not be thrown to the dogs!
Isaac, the innocent one, is a figure of this bread,
along with the Passover lamb and the mysterious manna.

Have compassion on us, good shepherd, true bread.
Feed us and keep us and lead us to heaven.
You are all-powerful and all-knowing, divine shepherd of sheep.
Grant us in heaven to enjoy the inheritance with you.

Amen.

content.value: Acclamation Before the Gospel (We Speak to God)

This acclamation is itself a rite, or rather an act, by which the assembly of the faithful welcomes and greets the Lord, who will speak to them in the Gospel, and by which it professes its faith through song. The verses are taken from the lectionary or from the [[Gradual|Gradual (Graduale Romanum)]].

The Alleluia is sung throughout the year, except during Lent, when it is omitted and replaced by an acclamatory verse. We know this verse as «honor and glory to you, Lord Jesus».

The word «Alleluia» comes from a Hebrew expression meaning «Praise the Lord!» or «praised be the Lord!». This word resembles forms of jubilation found among all peoples. It is a shout of acclamation to Christ, Teacher and Lord, who becomes present in the Gospel.

The Alleluia should be sung by the whole assembly; everyone should share in the joy of encountering the Lord who speaks. It is the whole assembly that sets out toward the Lord, acclaiming him with enthusiasm, in a shared communal and choral rhythm.

The most fruitful union between the Word and the Church takes place in the liturgical assembly in action, the privileged place where the Word of God becomes present and active, where the καιρός (kairos) of the Word occurs.

The Proclamation of the Gospel is the central and most important part of the entire **Liturgy of the Word**. This is shown by all the gestures and symbols that accompany this proclamation:


![img:fortunino-matania.jpg|right|w:50%|Fortunino Matania, the Sermon on the Mount]
- It has an Acclamation before it is announced.
- Its proclamation belongs properly to the ordained ministers, especially the deacon.
- When the Bishop presides, whoever will proclaim it, whether Deacon or Priest, asks him for a blessing.
- It has its own liturgical book: the Book of the Gospels.
- A procession carries the Book of the Gospels from the Altar to the Ambo, showing the bond between the two tables: the table of the Word and the table of the Eucharist.
- Incensation of the Word.
- Singing the Gospel is recommended, to lend greater solemnity to its proclamation.
- The Assembly listens to it standing.
- Its proclamation and hearing have the power to forgive venial sins.
- It is venerated with a kiss at the end of the proclamation.

This is the moment when the Church listens to and receives the announcement of Christ himself, because «God himself speaks to his people» and Christ, present in his own word, proclaims the Gospel.

The Gospel is read from the [[Book of the Gospels|Evangeliario]] on [[Sundays|Domingos, solemnidades y fiestas]], Solemnities, and Feasts. On the remaining days, the [[Lectionary|Leccionario]] is used.

content.title: Procession with the Book of the Gospels
content.value: If the Book of the Gospels is on the altar, he takes it and, preceded by the lay ministers who may carry the thurible and candles, goes to the ambo, carrying the Book of the Gospels slightly raised. Those present turn toward the ambo to show special reverence for the Gospel of Christ.

content.title: The Sunday Cycle
content.value:
The Sunday system is divided into three annual cycles called A, B, and C. In them, during Ordinary Time, the first reading is always from the Old Testament and is chosen in relation to the Gospel; the second is apostolic and follows its own semi-continuous course; and the third reading, the Gospel, likewise semi-continuous, is taken from Matthew in Year A, Mark in Year B, and Luke in Year C. Chapter VI of John is read on the Sundays of Weeks XVII to XXI of Cycle B.

In the special seasons —Advent, Christmas, Lent, and Easter— the readings have been chosen to follow and live out the spirit of the liturgical season.

content.title: Weekday Cycle
content.value:
The Gospel reading is taken from the guiding evangelist of the year. John is read at the end of Lent and during the Easter Season, and throughout this season the Acts of the Apostles is read both on Sundays and on weekdays.

In the weekday readings (ferias), of which there are only two, books or series of books of the Old and New Testament are read alternately in two alternating cycles: even years and odd years. The Gospel readings, however, are repeated: each year Mark, Matthew, and Luke are read in succession.

The Homily is a living liturgical act and part of the celebration itself, through which the ordained minister explains the Sacred Scriptures that have been proclaimed, or the texts of the day's Mass. In the homily the priest explains to us the true meaning of the Scriptures, makes explicit the message God is giving us, makes the proclaimed Word more accessible to us, and opens us to the Mystery of Christ.

It is strictly obligatory on Sundays and holy days of obligation and is reserved exclusively to the [[Bishop|Obispo]], the [[Priest|Presbítero]] (priest), or the [[Deacon|Diácono]]. A layperson may not give the homily within the eucharistic celebration. (Cf. GIRM {{66|qolj09|66}}; Redemptionis Sacramentum 64-66).

It was the Second Vatican Council that restored to the Word of God its rightful importance: «In sacred celebrations there is to be more reading from holy scripture, and it is to be more varied and suitable.» (SC 35), going so far as to affirm that «Christ is always present in His Church, especially in her liturgical celebrations.… He is present in His word, since it is He Himself who speaks when the holy scriptures are read in the Church.»
content.author: SC 7 (cf. CCC 1088)

content.value:
It might seem contradictory that _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (cf. _SC_ 30) tells us that, to promote active participation in the Assembly, sacred silence should be observed at the proper times, since for us silence seems something passive, a mere absence of sound.

The Introduction to the Lectionary for Mass says: «The dialogue between God and his people taking place through the Holy Spirit demands short intervals of silence, suited to the assembly, as an opportunity to take the word of God to heart and to prepare a response to it in prayer.» (OLM 28).

Sacred silence is the «moment of the Spirit». We live in a world full of internal and external noise; we need silence to encounter God, to listen to him, so that his Word may resound within us and we may let the Spirit act in us.

The profession of faith or creed (_Symbolum_) is a brief, normative formula with which the Church sums up and hands on the content of the Christian faith. It is called a «creed» because it usually begins with the Latin word _credo_ (I believe); it is also called the «symbol of faith». It has its origin in the personal profession of faith made by the catechumen about to be baptized. It is not, properly speaking, a prayer —we do not address God or ask him for anything— but rather a public profession of what we believe. It is sung or recited on [[Sundays and Solemnities|domingos, solemnidades y fiestas]].

![img:Rafael-La-Pesca-Milagrosa.jpg|right|w:50%|Raphael, the Miraculous Catch of Fish]
In the Mass, the _Symbolum_ has a purpose: that the assembled people may respond to the Word proclaimed in the readings and explained in the homily, and that, by pronouncing the rule of faith in an approved formula, they may recall and confess the great mysteries of the faith before celebrating them in the Eucharist.

There are two formulas. The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed is proposed first and used ordinarily. The Apostles' Creed —shorter, and linked by its origin to the baptismal profession— may be used as an alternative "for the benefit of the faithful", especially during Lent and the Fifty Days of Easter.

**In both formulas there is a gesture that is often overlooked:** upon reaching the words that announce the Incarnation —_«and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man»_ in the Nicene Creed; _«who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary»_ in the Apostles' Creed— all are to bow their heads. On the Solemnities of the Annunciation and of the Nativity of the Lord, a genuflection is made instead of a bow.

The «Universal Prayer» (also called the Prayer of the Faithful) is the element with which the Liturgy of the Word concludes in the Mass. In it the people, exercising the office of their baptismal priesthood, respond to the Word of God received in faith by offering petitions to God for the salvation of all.

The General Instruction of the Roman Missal (cf. _GIRM_ {{69|qolj09|69}}) establishes that this prayer is ordinarily to take place in Masses celebrated with a congregation, and that the petitions are to be made for:

- The needs of the Church.
- Those who govern and the salvation of the world.
- Those oppressed by any kind of difficulty.
- The local community.

In particular celebrations —such as Confirmation, Marriage, or [[funeral rites|Exequias]]— this order may be adapted to give more explicit place to the occasion.

The celebrant priest directs the petitions (intentions) from the chair: he introduces them with a brief invitation for the faithful to pray, and concludes them with a prayer. 

The intentions themselves —which should be sober, composed with wise freedom and few words— are proposed by the deacon, or else by a cantor, a lector, or a member of the lay faithful, from the ambo or from another suitable place. The people, standing, respond to each intention with a common invocation, or else pray in silence.
«Christian charity extends without end in the Mass, reaching all people».

subsections.title: Liturgy of the Eucharist
subsections.subtitle: Offertory | Prayer over the Offerings | Eucharistic Prayer | Breaking of the Bread and Communion

content.value:
Christ, then, took the bread and the chalice, gave thanks, broke the bread, and gave them to his disciples, saying: Take, eat, drink; this is my Body; this is the chalice of my Blood. Do this in memory of me. Accordingly, the Church has arranged the entire celebration of the **Liturgy of the Eucharist** in these parts, corresponding to the words and actions of Christ, namely:

1. At the **Preparation of the Gifts**, the bread and the wine with water are brought to the altar, that is, the very elements that Christ took into his hands.
2. In the **Eucharistic Prayer**, thanks is given to God for the whole work of salvation, and the offerings become the Body and Blood of Christ.
3. Through the **breaking of the bread and through Communion**, the faithful, though they are many, receive the Lord's Body from the one bread and the Lord's Blood from the one chalice, in the same way the Apostles received them from Christ's own hands.

subsections.title: Preparation of the Gifts (Offertory)
keyPoints: Preparation of the Chalice (The Water and the Wine)

content.value:
This merely preparatory part was extremely simple in the early Church. The rite grew and became increasingly important over time. Already by the seventh century there was a procession to carry the gifts to the [[altar|Altar]]. The faithful brought bread and wine and other gifts for the community's support and works of charity. Later the gifts were no longer given in kind but in money, as remains the practice today. Private prayers of the presider and other rites, such as the washing of hands, were added.

As soon as the Prayer of the Faithful concludes, the assembly sits, and the presider does likewise together with the concelebrants. The procession with the gifts begins, along with the chant that accompanies it — a chant that continues until the priest has purified his hands.

While the faithful present the offerings (or the collection is taken up), the acolyte or the ministers place the [[corporal|corporal]], the [[purificator|purificador]], the [[Missal|Misal Romano]], and the [[chalice|cáliz]] on the altar. 

The altar becomes the table of the Lord's banquet and the place of sacrifice.

The gifts carried in this procession are bread and wine, which will become the Body and Blood of Christ: the unleavened bread in [[ciboria|copón]] or [[patens|patena]], and the wine together with the water in the [[cruets|vinajeras]]. It is praiseworthy for the faithful themselves to present them; although today they no longer bring the bread and wine from their own possessions as was done in the past, the rite of presenting them still retains its force and its spiritual significance. Money or other gifts for the poor or for the church may also be received at this time and placed in a suitable location, **apart from the eucharistic table.**

The presider may receive the gifts in front of the altar or at the [[chair|Sede]].

This procession in which the gifts are carried is accompanied by the offertory chant, which continues at least until the gifts have been placed on the altar. The norms governing how it is sung are the same as for the entrance chant. It is a chant from the [[Proper|Propio]], meaning its text may vary according to the liturgical season or celebration; it should speak of bread and wine, of gifts, of oblation, of self-giving — thereby supporting the prayer the assembly makes at this moment. The chant may always accompany the offertory rite, even without a procession with the gifts.

content.title: Recommendations
content.value: It is quite common in some celebrations, such as weddings or quinceañeras, for the “Ave Maria” to be sung, which, besides not being a liturgical chant, has nothing to do with this celebratory moment and completely disrupts its flow, turning it, as we have already noted, into a spectacle. This is why we must avoid anything that disrupts the harmony of the eucharistic celebration.

Even though the faithful no longer bring from their own possessions the bread and wine intended for the liturgy as in the past, nevertheless the rite of carrying up the offerings still retains its force and its spiritual significance.
content.author: GIRM 73

content.value:
The priest takes the paten with the bread and, holding it slightly raised above the altar, says quietly:

`Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the bread we offer you: fruit of the earth and work of human hands, it will become for us the bread of life.`


If there is no singing during the presentation of the gifts, the priest may say these words aloud; at the end the people acclaim:

`Blessed be God for ever.`


Afterward, the priest places the paten with the bread on the corporal.

content.title: Did You Know?
content.value:
In general, it is called bread or unleavened bread before the consecration, and host or consecrated host after the consecration. 

In Latin, 'hostia' is synonymous with victim.

content.title: Identify This Moment
content.text: The priest raises the paten with the bread and says a few words quietly.

content.value: Preparation of the Chalice (The Water and the Wine)

The deacon, or the priest, pours wine and a little water into the chalice, saying quietly:

`By the mystery of this water and wine, may we come to share in the divinity of Christ, who humbled himself to share in our humanity.`


The wine represents the divinity of Christ and the water our humanity. By mixing them, we ask that our human nature be raised up and united to his divine nature.

Then the priest takes the chalice and, holding it slightly raised above the altar, says quietly:

`Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the wine we offer you: fruit of the vine and work of human hands, it will become our spiritual drink.`


If there is no singing during the presentation of the gifts, the priest may say these words aloud; at the end the people may acclaim:

`Blessed be God for ever.`


Afterward he places the chalice on the corporal.

content.title: Identify This Moment
content.text: The priest slightly raises the chalice and says a few words quietly.

content.value:
Then the priest, bowing, says quietly:

`With humble spirit and contrite heart, may we be accepted by you, O Lord, and may our sacrifice in your sight this day be pleasing to you, Lord God.`


With this bodily bow and intimate prayer, the priest expresses his own littleness and attitude of penance (together with that of the assembled People of God) before the holiness of God. He acknowledges that the sacrifice will be pleasing to God not because of the minister's own merits or personal worthiness, but through the grace of Christ, uniting the humble heart of the whole assembly to the sacrifice of Christ, the one true High Priest.

The priest incenses the gifts, the cross, and the altar. Then the deacon or the thurifer (the minister who carries the thurible) incenses the priest and, finally, the assembly.

The minister bows to the faithful before and after incensing them, because the liturgical assembly is also the mystical body and a living presence of God.

Just as with the bread and wine on the altar, the priest offers himself, and with him the whole community is enveloped in the same incense. In this way, the prayers of the Church rise up to God, and all those present become a holy offering and a living sacrifice, united and incorporated into the one sacrifice of Christ.

The priest washes his hands at the side of the altar, a rite that expresses the desire for interior purification. Before purifying himself, he says one prayer quietly, and another during the washing of his hands, while the minister pours the water:

`Wash me, O Lord, from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.`

Standing at the center of the altar and facing the people, extending and then joining his hands, the priest invites the people to pray with the invitation ("Pray, brethren..."), which prompts the whole assembly to stand immediately:

**Priest:**

`Pray, brethren (brothers and sisters), that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to God, the almighty Father.`


**People's response:**

`May the Lord accept the sacrifice at your hands for the praise and glory of his name, for our good and the good of all his holy Church.`


Then the priest, with hands extended, says the prayer over the offerings.

The prayer over the offerings has a theme properly of oblation, in which God the Father is asked to accept the gifts we present for the sacrifice and to accept us ourselves as a pleasing offering.

content.text: The priest raises his hands, and everyone stands as he says "Pray, brethren..."

subsections.tag: Liturgy of the Eucharist, Part II
subsections.title: The Eucharistic Prayer

content.value:
The Eucharistic Prayer, also called the anaphora or great Eucology, is the most important and principal prayer of the Holy Mass. It begins with the **Preface** and ends with the **final Doxology**, solemnly sealed by the people's Great Amen.

Now the center and summit of the entire celebration begins: the Eucharistic Prayer, which is indeed a prayer of thanksgiving and sanctification. The priest invites the people to lift up their hearts to the Lord in prayer and thanksgiving, and unites them with himself in the prayer that he addresses, in the name of the whole community, to God the Father, through Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit. The meaning of this prayer is that the entire assembly of the faithful should join itself with Christ in confessing the wonders of God and in the offering of the sacrifice. **The Eucharistic Prayer demands that all listen to it with reverence and in silence.**

The Preface is the thanksgiving that the Church offers to God the Father for the wonders accomplished in Jesus for our salvation. **To give thanks** is _eucaristein_ in Greek, from which the word **"Eucharist"** derives — one of the oldest and most expressive names for the Holy Mass. It opens with an introductory dialogue between the celebrant and the assembly, in which we are invited to the prayer of thanksgiving, always and everywhere, as something right and just for our salvation.

**Priest** (with hands extended): _The Lord be with you._
**Assembly**: _And with your spirit._
**Priest** (raising his hands): _Lift up your hearts._
**Assembly**: _We lift them up to the Lord._
**Priest** (with hands extended): _Let us give thanks to the Lord our God._
**Assembly**: _It is right and just._
**Priest**: _It is truly right and just..._
_(The priest continues the Preface with hands extended.)_

Examples of Prefaces:

tabs.label: PREFACE I OF CHRISTMAS
tabs.value:
(Christ, the Light of the world)
It is truly right and just,
our duty and our salvation,

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
The purpose of the Preface is to thank God for every gift and every work he has freely accomplished for our salvation. That is why it opens with that most ancient dialogue: "It is truly right and just to give you thanks" — not a mere formality, but a duty that springs from the believing heart.

As the Catechism teaches, in the Preface the Church acknowledges before the Father, through Christ and in the Spirit, the whole of his saving work: having created, having redeemed, and having sanctified (Cf. CCC 1352).

This attitude that we express in the Holy Mass cannot remain at the altar: it must be carried into all of life. Saint Paul asked this of the first Christians: "give thanks in all circumstances" (1 Thess 5:18), because God is continually helping and guiding us, even when we do not notice it.

Saint John Chrysostom, one of the great preachers of the Eucharist, summed up this attitude in his last words before he died in exile: "Glory to God for all things!" (Palladius, Life of Saint John Chrysostom, 11).

_"Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of hosts. Heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest."_

The singing of the Sanctus was introduced into the eucharistic celebration in the fourth century in the East and in the fifth century in the West. It is an expression of recognition of the greatness and holiness of God. It is an acclamation that unites the Church on earth with the Church in heaven. It is the oldest and most important chant in the repertoire of chants of the [[Ordinary|Ordinario]].

It is a prayer composed, in part, of the words the prophet Isaiah heard the seraphim sing (Is 6:2-3), and in part drawn from the praise with which the crowd acclaimed Jesus as he entered Jerusalem (Mt 21:9).

It is a way of welcoming Jesus Christ, who will become present in the eucharistic species of bread and wine that will become his Body and his Blood. The choir should encourage the assembly to sing, and must fully respect the original text of the Sanctus as it is written in the Missal.

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
To praise him is to recognize that everything we are, we are thanks to him, to his love, and to his desire to save us. That is why the Sanctus is not just any hymn: it is the acclamation with which, joining the heavenly choirs, we proclaim the holiness of God (Cf. GIRM 79b), just as the seraphim proclaimed it before the prophet Isaiah: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord" (Is 6:3).

Saint John Chrysostom described this moment in these words: "The angels surround the priest; the whole sanctuary... is filled with the heavenly hosts of angels who honor God, present at the altar."

Saint Augustine opens his Confessions this way, almost as if teaching us how to pray the Sanctus: "Great are you, O Lord, and greatly to be praised" (Confessions, I, 1, 1). And he immediately gives the ultimate reason for that praise: "You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." That is what we contemplate in the Sanctus: that we come from God, that his works are great and worthy of an almighty God who loves us, and that only in him does the heart find rest.

The word epiclesis comes from the Greek _epí_ (επι), meaning "upon," and _kaleo_ (καλεω), meaning "to call, to invoke." 

It is the invocation the priest makes to God the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon the gifts of bread and wine, so that he may transform them into the Body and Blood of Christ. The gesture the priest performs is the laying on of hands, holding them extended over the offerings — the epicletic gesture par excellence. Although the epiclesis is the invocation of the Holy Spirit, it also has a Trinitarian dimension, since it is the Father who sends the Spirit through his Son Jesus Christ.

Shortly before the consecration, the minister, if deemed appropriate, may alert the faithful with a ring of the bell, and likewise at each elevation, according to local custom.

Example, Eucharistic Prayer II:

`"You are indeed Holy, O Lord, the fount of all holiness; make holy, therefore, these gifts, we pray, by sending down your Spirit upon them like the dewfall, so that they may become for us the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ."`

content.title: Identify This Moment
content.text: The priest extends his hands over the bread and wine, and we kneel. There may be a ring of the bell.

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
The Eucharist is, in a certain sense, a prolongation of the Lord's Incarnation: the Church teaches that it "is at the same time in continuity with the Incarnation" (John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia, 55). Just as, by the action of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, the Word became flesh, so too now, by the action of that same Holy Spirit — invoked in this first epiclesis so that the gifts of bread and wine may become the Body and Blood of Christ (Cf. GIRM 79c) — Christ becomes present in the heart of the Church under the eucharistic species.

Saint Thomas Aquinas summed up this same parallel in the hymn he composed for Corpus Christi: "The Word made flesh, by his word, turns true bread into his flesh" (Pange Lingua, stanza 4). The same Word who became flesh in Mary's womb is the one who now, with his word, makes his Body present once again upon the altar.*

Saint Augustine, for his part, reminded the faithful that the Lord "received his flesh from the flesh of Mary" (Expositions on the Psalms, 98, 4).

*Thomas Aquinas wrote this hymn at the request of Pope Urban IV in 1264, precisely to institute the feast of Corpus Christi following the eucharistic miracle of Bolsena

The priest begins to narrate to God the Father — not to the assembly — what Jesus Christ, his Son, did and said at the Last Supper with his apostles. When pronouncing the words of Christ _"Take this, all of you, and eat of it..."_, _"Take this, all of you, and drink from it..."_, he should make a slight bow and not show the species to the assembly as if he were speaking to them.

![flip:square|50|right|Sta_Maria_Guadalupe_Consagracion.jpg~|text|TAKE THIS, ALL OF YOU, AND EAT OF IT~~light]
It is at the moment the priest pronounces these words of Christ that, by their efficacy and by the action of the Holy Spirit invoked in the epiclesis, the [[transubstantiation|Transubstanciación]] occurs: the bread and wine become really and substantially the Body and Blood of Christ.

Immediately after pronouncing the words over the bread, the priest shows the consecrated host to the people, then places it on the paten and adores it by genuflecting. After pronouncing the words over the chalice, he shows it to the people, then places it on the corporal and adores it by genuflecting.

This moment ends with the **priest** saying:

`The mystery of faith.`

And the **people** continue with one of the following acclamations:

`We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again.`


Or:

`When we eat this Bread and drink this Cup, we proclaim your Death, O Lord, until you come again.`


Or:

`Save us, Savior of the world, for by your Cross and Resurrection you have set us free.`

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
What are you doing with your eyes closed or fixed on the floor? Lift up your gaze and contemplate Christ elevated on the altar!

These are not cold memories of past events. The Catechism teaches that the biblical memorial is not merely to recall the past, but to make present, in some way, the wonders God worked for us (Cf. CCC 1363). That is why the Council of Trent could affirm that the sacrifice of the cross and that of this altar are one and the same: "only the manner of offering is different" (CCC 1367, quoting Trent, Session 22, ch. 2).

What you are contemplating is not a symbol or a theatrical re-enactment: it is Christ himself, the same Calvary, made present here and now... "do this in remembrance of me" (Lk 22:19).

At the Last Supper our Savior instituted the Eucharistic Sacrifice of his Body and Blood, by which he would perpetuate the Sacrifice of the Cross throughout the centuries until he should come again, thus entrusting to the Church, his beloved Bride, the memorial of his death and resurrection.
content.author: GIRM 2

content.value:
_"Anamnesis: In which the Church, fulfilling the command that she received from Christ the Lord through the Apostles, keeps the memorial of Christ, recalling especially his blessed Passion, glorious Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven"_ (GIRM 79e).

The word "anamnesis" comes from the Greek _anámnesis_, meaning "to make memory." In the liturgy, it makes the past become present — actualized — and the future become present — anticipated, foretasted. In the Holy Mass, Christ's paschal banquet and his redemptive sacrifice on the cross are made present; that is why the [[altar|Altar]] is a symbol of the upper room and of Golgotha, and the community shares in advance in the eternal banquet of heaven, in the heavenly liturgy. This is not a cold recollection of past events, but a living memory carried out _hic et nunc_ (here and now). Jesus not only said "do this," but also added: "in memory of me."

Eucharistic Prayer II (Memorial):

`"Therefore, as we celebrate the memorial of his Death and Resurrection, we offer you, Lord, the Bread of life and the Chalice of salvation, giving thanks that you have held us worthy to be in your presence and minister to you."`

_"Offering: By which, in this very memorial, the Church — and in particular the Church here and now gathered — offers in the Holy Spirit the spotless Victim to the Father. The Church's intention, however, is that the faithful not only offer this spotless Victim but also learn to offer themselves, and so day by day be consummated, through Christ the Mediator, into unity with God and with each other, so that at last God may be all in all"_ (GIRM 79f).

The true offertory is here. As the Lord's sacrificial and sanctifying action becomes present to us in the memorial, we offer the Father the perfect Victim: Christ. We unite ourselves to that offering.

Section 34 of Lumen Gentium teaches us how Jesus, the supreme and perfect priest, the Christ, the Anointed of the Spirit, has fulfilled his priestly action of perfect praise to the Father and of the sanctification of mankind in his offering consummated on the cross, which today becomes present to us in the Eucharist. But Jesus has willed to associate with his own priestly offering all who are united to him through Baptism, and for this he gives them his Holy Spirit, who identifies and transforms them into him.

Some examples, according to the Eucharistic Prayer:
**Prayer I**: _"we offer you this sacrifice of praise, or they offer it for themselves and all who are dear to them..."_
**Prayer II**: _"we offer you the Bread of life and the Chalice of salvation..."_
**Prayer III**: _"we offer you in thanksgiving this holy and living sacrifice. Look, we pray, upon the oblation of your Church… may he make of us an eternal offering to you."_
**Prayer IV**: _"we offer you his Body and Blood, the sacrifice acceptable to you which brings salvation to the whole world..."_


^^In the full text of the Missal, the Offering and the Second Epiclesis usually form a single continuous prayer, without a full stop between them (as happens, for example, in Prayer III). The distinction between these two elements is a theological categorization from the GIRM (no. {{79|qolj09|79}}), useful for study, but it does not always correspond to a visible separation in the printed text of each Prayer.^^

The action of the Holy Spirit is invoked once again, so that he may transform the assembly gathered there into one body whose head is Christ.

This _epiclesis_ asks the Spirit to bring about in the assembly what Jesus asked the Father to bring about in his Church (Jn 17:20-21). While in the first _epiclesis_ the Spirit acts immediately, changing the bread into the Body and the wine into the Blood of Christ, in the second the Spirit's action reaches its completion at the moment of Communion — that is, when the faithful enter into sacramental communion with the Body of Christ (the host) and with the Body of Christ (the assembly).

**Prayer II**: _"Humbly we pray that, partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ, we may be gathered into one by the Holy Spirit."_
**Prayer III**: _"...that we, who are nourished by the Body and Blood of your Son and filled with his Holy Spirit, may become one body, one spirit in Christ."_
**Prayer IV**: _"...and grant in your loving kindness to all who partake of this one Bread and one Chalice that, gathered into one body by the Holy Spirit, they may truly become a living sacrifice in Christ to the praise of your glory."_
**Prayer I (Roman Canon)**: _"In humble prayer we ask you, almighty God: command that these gifts be borne by the hands of your holy Angel to your altar on high in the sight of your divine majesty, so that all of us, who through this participation at the altar receive the most holy Body and Blood of your Son, may be filled with every grace and heavenly blessing."_


^^Eucharistic Prayer I (or Roman Canon) has a particular structure. Instead of a single explicit invocation of the Holy Spirit upon the gifts and then upon the faithful, the Roman Canon makes the invocation implicitly through this prayer to the angels, so that the assembled congregation may receive the fruits of Communion.^^
It is necessary that, when we celebrate this eucharistic sacrifice, we ourselves be immolated to God in contrition of heart...
content.author: Saint Gregory the Great (Dialogues, IV, 61, 1).

content.value:
This part of the Prayer richly expresses ecclesial unity, as it asks for all the needs of **the Church on earth (the pilgrim Church)**. It prays for the Universal Church, beginning with her pastors (the Pope, the Bishop). It then prays for the assembly gathered there, that one day, together with **the Church in purgatory**, it may share with **the Church triumphant** (the Virgin Mary, Saint Joseph, and all the saints) in the eternal glory of heaven.

**Prayer II**: _"Remember, Lord, your Church, spread throughout the world, and bring her to the fullness of charity, together with N. our Pope and N. our Bishop and all the clergy. Remember also our brothers and sisters who have fallen asleep in the hope of the resurrection, and all who have died in your mercy: welcome them into the light of your face. Have mercy on us all, we pray, that with the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with Saint Joseph, her Spouse, with the blessed Apostles, and all the Saints who have pleased you throughout the ages, we may merit to be coheirs to eternal life, and may praise and glorify you through your Son, Jesus Christ."_


^^While in the Prayer of the Faithful we pray explicitly for the whole world — for the needs of the Church, for those who govern and for the salvation of the world, for those who suffer any hardship, and for the local community (GIRM 70) — in the Eucharistic Prayer the intercessions have a properly ecclesial character: they express that the Eucharist is celebrated in communion with the whole Church, in heaven and on earth, and that the oblation is offered for her and for all her members, living and dead (GIRM 79g). There is no explicit petition here for those who govern or for world peace, as there is in the Prayer of the Faithful; although in Prayer IV, which prays "for all your holy people **and for those who seek you with a sincere heart**" — there is a discreet formula that includes, without naming them as such, those who sincerely seek God without belonging to the Church.^^

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
Saint Augustine recounts that his mother, Saint Monica, on her deathbed, asked neither for a solemn burial nor for a marked tomb, but for something far simpler: "only this I ask of you, that you remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you may be" (Confessions, IX, 27). She knew what you can discover now: that there is no more powerful place to remember those we love than this altar.

Saint John Chrysostom taught his flock the same thing: "let us not hesitate to help those who have died" (Homilies on the First Letter to the Corinthians, 41, 5; quoted in CCC 1032). That is why, when the priest says "Remember also, Lord, your children...", that is your moment: name in the silence of your heart those who are no longer with you.
