content.value:
The Greek word doxa (_δοξα_) means "glory." The doxology is the final glorification of the entire prayer of thanksgiving (the Eucharistic Prayer).

The priest says: 

`"Through him, and with him, and in him, O God, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all glory and honor is yours, for ever and ever."`

The people acclaim: 

`"Amen."`


The doxology is, without doubt, the crown of the Eucharistic Prayer. It is a brief hymn glorifying the Father, and the Son, through the Holy Spirit.

It is highly recommended that the doxology be sung, to give it greater prominence as a joyful element of glorification. The concelebrating priests join the presider in reciting it and, at this point, may do so aloud. The presider raises the Body and Blood of Christ with arms fully extended, since this is the greatest of all the elevations.

content.title: Identify This Moment
content.text: The priest raises the chalice and the paten with the host together.

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
Only "through him, and with him, and in him" can we reach the Father. Our lives, united to his life, his death, and his resurrection, are honor and glory to the Trinity. Saint Augustine preached this same truth to his people: "God-as-Christ is the homeland we are going to; Christ-as-man is the way by which we go" (Sermon 123, 3).

The Church exists to glorify God: that is why the entire Eucharistic Prayer culminates precisely in this acclamation of glory, sealed by the "Amen" of the whole people (Cf. GIRM 79h).

The doxology, and the entire Eucharistic Prayer, conclude with the people's acclamation "Amen." The word "Amen" expresses our assent (acceptance) and our total adherence to everything that has been done and said in the Eucharistic Prayer. It is a true response that expresses our faith. We should not replace the word "Amen" with other expressions such as "so be it," "I believe," etc.

Of all the "Amens" we say at Mass, this is the greatest and most important, because of its context and because it is set within the Eucharistic Prayer. It is recommended that it be sung in a solemn manner.

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
May our "Great Amen" at Mass be the response we give to God for the work of redemption accomplished in us through Christ: a generous "yes," full of trust in every circumstance, acknowledging that everything is for his glory.

Saint Augustine taught the newly baptized the weight of that small word: "to that which you are, you respond 'Amen,' and by responding, you sign your name to it" (Sermon 272). Saying "Amen" is not merely listening and assenting: it is putting your own life's signature on what God has just accomplished at the altar. May your Great Amen, then, be not an automatic murmur, but a true signature.

Let us recall that the Eucharistic liturgy has as its backbone what Christ did and said at the Last Supper with his apostles, in order to perpetuate his Paschal Mystery and to make memorial of him each time we gather in his name. 

_“He took bread (Presentation of the Gifts), gave thanks (Eucharistic Prayer), broke it (Breaking of the Bread), and gave it (Communion).”_

Since the Eucharistic Celebration is the Paschal Banquet, it is desirable that in keeping with the Lord's command, his Body and Blood should be received as spiritual food by the faithful who are properly disposed. This is the sense of the fraction and the other preparatory rites by which the faithful are led directly to Communion.
content.author: GIRM 80

content.value:
Immediately after the Great Amen, the Communion Rite begins with the Lord's Prayer. What we do is say to Jesus, _“teach us to pray,”_ and he teaches us and, through us, begins to pray. **Let us recall that Jesus, at this very moment, is present with us in the consecrated host and wine.**

This prayer is introduced by an invitation that the priest says, either one provided in the Roman Missal or one he may improvise himself:

`“At the Savior's command and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say:”`


The priest, with hands extended, says the Lord's Prayer together with the people.

It is also known as the “Dominical Prayer” — that is, the prayer of the Lord (_Dominus_, in Latin) — the same root as the word “Sunday” (_dies dominica_, the Lord's Day).

In the Lord's Prayer we ask for our daily bread —which for Christians signifies above all the Eucharistic bread— and we implore the purification of sins, so that holy things may be given to the holy.

**It is composed of seven petitions:**
1. Hallowed be thy name.
2. Thy kingdom come.
3. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
4. Give us this day our daily bread.
5. Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.
6. Lead us not into temptation.
7. And deliver us from evil.

Although it is the prayer Christ himself taught, and it holds great importance in the liturgy —it is recommended to pray it three times a day, as in the early Church (Mass, Lauds, and Vespers)—, **it is not the most important prayer of the Holy Mass**: that place belongs to the Eucharistic Prayer.


^^The Missal only indicates that the priest raises his hands and says this prayer together with the people, without specifying the posture of the faithful. The gesture of holding hands, proper to the Rite of Peace, does not belong to this moment; and raising one's arms is, in its origin, a priestly gesture of intercession, though it also has ancient testimony among the faithful in catacomb art.^^

The embolism is the prayer the priest says immediately after the Lord's Prayer, developing and extending its final petition, _“deliver us from evil”_ (GIRM {{81|qolj09|81}}).

**Priest:** 

`“Deliver us, Lord, we pray, from every evil, graciously grant peace in our days, that, by the help of your mercy, we may be always free from sin and safe from all distress, as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Savior, Jesus Christ.”`

The **people** conclude, acclaiming: 

`“For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and for ever.”`


^^The word “embolism” comes from the Greek _embolismós_, “to insert” or “to interpolate.”^^

With the Rite of Peace, _“the Church asks for peace and unity for herself and for the whole human family, and the faithful express to each other their ecclesial communion and mutual charity before communicating in the Sacrament”_ (GIRM {{82|qolj09|82}}).

**After the embolism, the priest says:** 

`“Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles: 'Peace I leave you, my peace I give you…'”`

**and the people respond at the end:** 

`“Amen.”`

**Then the priest says:** 

`“The peace of the Lord be with you always”`

**and the people respond:** 

`“And with your spirit.”`

**Then the deacon, or the priest, adds:** 

`“Let us offer each other the sign of peace.”`

(or some other formula provided in the Missal).


The Roman Missal does not provide for any singing at this moment; therefore, no singing should be done. **Nor should the Agnus Dei be begun early.**

It suffices to offer the sign of peace to those nearby, to express that we are doing so together with the whole assembly, rather than going around giving the peace to everyone.


^^The Rite of Peace does not carry a sense of reconciliation or forgiveness of sins, but rather signifies peace, communion, and charity before receiving the Eucharist. The sense of reconciliation among brothers and sisters was already expressed earlier, in the Penitential Act.^^

content.title: Take Note
content.text: Many people miss the moment of the breaking of the bread by prolonging the Rite of Peace.

content.value:
The priest breaks the Eucharistic bread, with the help, where appropriate, of the deacon or a concelebrant. Christ's gesture of breaking the bread at the Last Supper, which in apostolic times designated the entire Eucharistic action, signifies that the faithful, though many, are made one body (1 Cor 10:17) in the Communion of the one Bread of life, who is Christ, dead and risen for the salvation of the world. The fraction begins after the sign of peace has been exchanged and is carried out with due reverence.

**The priest breaks the host into three parts** and drops one of them (the smallest) into the chalice, saying quietly:

`“May this mingling of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ bring eternal life to us who receive it.”`


![img:d2d78f2b2d457cb32383b28c3f6732c1-2.jpg|right|w:45%]
This small particle has been called, since antiquity, the _fermentum_, and the action is called the _commingling_. It signifies the unity of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the work of redemption.

During the breaking of the bread, the Agnus Dei is sung, either by the cantors, or by the cantor followed by the response of the people, or at least it is recited aloud: 

`Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.`

If the breaking of the bread continues for some time, the preceding invocation may be repeated several times. The last time, it concludes: grant us peace.

content.title: Contemplate
content.value:
In the breaking of the bread, the sign is divided, but Christ gives himself whole to each person. In receiving him, we do not fragment him: rather, it is we who are gathered together in Him.

This is not merely a pious intuition: it is the very doctrine that St. Thomas Aquinas set to verse in the hymn Lauda Sion, which the Church sings on the solemnity of Corpus Christi: "Fracto demum Sacramento, ne vacilles, sed memento tantum esse sub fragmento quantum toto tegitur. Nulla rei fit scissura: signi tantum fit fractura" — that is: when the Sacrament is broken, do not waver, but remember that there is as much beneath the fragment as in the whole; the reality is not divided, only the sign is broken (Lauda Sion, verses 19-20).

For this reason, in every particle of the host, however small, and in every drop in the chalice, the living and glorious Jesus Christ is present, with his Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity. This is how the Council of Trent defines it: “If anyone denies that, in the venerable sacrament of the Eucharist, the whole Christ is contained under each of the species, and under every part of each species when separated, let him be anathema” (Council of Trent, Session 13, Canon 3).

**Preparation and Showing of the Host**
The priest prepares himself to receive the Body and Blood of Christ fruitfully with a quiet prayer. The faithful do the same, praying in silence.

The priest **shows the faithful the Eucharistic Bread** over the paten or the chalice, and invites them to the banquet of Christ, saying:

`“Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb.”`

And, together with the **people**, he makes an act of humility:

`“Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed.”`

![img:716353236-18104048093101198-2807024506901054998-n.jpg|right|w:50%]
**The Communion of the Priest and of the Faithful**
“While the priest is receiving the Sacrament, the Communion chant is begun. Its purpose is to express the communicants' union in spirit by means of the unity of their voices, to show joy of heart, and to highlight more clearly the 'communitarian' nature of the procession to receive Communion. The singing is continued for as long as the Sacrament is being administered to the faithful” (GIRM 86).

Then he takes the paten or the pyx, approaches those who wish to receive Communion, and presents the consecrated bread to each of them... saying to each one: _“The Body of Christ.”_ The one receiving Communion responds: _“Amen.”_

**Posture and Manner of Receiving Communion**
Communion may be received standing or kneeling, on the tongue or in the hand. If received in the hand, it must be consumed there, in front of the priest or minister of Communion. A bow or genuflection may be made before receiving it, but this should not be done at the very moment of receiving Communion, rather a little before.

Those in the Communion procession, as well as those who are seated, should sing the chant proper to this moment. **After receiving, the communicant must rejoin the prayer of the whole assembly** —that is, the Communion chant— and should not withdraw from the assembly to go toward the tabernacle. One may remain standing, kneel, or sit.


^^For the Communion chant, the antiphon from the Roman [[Gradual|Gradual (Graduale Romanum)]], with or without its psalm, may be used, or the antiphon with the psalm from the Simple Gradual, or some other suitable chant approved by the Conference of Bishops... when there is no singing, the antiphon given in the Missal may be said (GIRM 87).^^

content.title: To Pray After Communion
content.value:
Prayer of Thanksgiving of St. Thomas Aquinas:

I give you thanks, Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who have deigned—though I am a sinner and your unworthy servant, with no merit of my own but solely through your mercy—to nourish me with the Body and Blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

I beg you that this Holy Communion not become for my soul an occasion of condemnation, but a saving plea for forgiveness. May this Holy Communion be for me armor of faith, a shield of good will, the death of my vices, the banishment of all my carnal desires, and an increase of charity, patience, and every virtue.

May it be a worthy defense against all the enemies of my soul. May it be a perfect remedy for my spirit, a lasting friendship with you, my true God and Lord, and the seal of my blessed death.

I ask you to be pleased to bring this sinner to that ineffable banquet where you, with your Son and the Holy Spirit, are for all your saints true light, perfect fulfillment, everlasting joy, consummate happiness, and perfect bliss. Amen.

The Mass is at the same time, and inseparably, the sacrificial memorial in which the sacrifice of the cross is perpetuated and the sacred banquet of communion with the Lord's body and blood. But the celebration of the Eucharistic sacrifice is wholly directed toward the intimate union of the faithful with Christ through communion. To receive communion is to receive Christ himself who has offered himself for us.

content.title: Purification of the Vessels
content.value:
Once the distribution of Communion has ended, before anything else, the priest himself, at the altar, drinks entirely any consecrated wine that may remain; but any consecrated hosts that remain are either consumed at the altar or carried to the place designated for reserving the Eucharist.

After Communion, the deacon, the acolyte, or the priest himself purifies the paten or the ciborium over the chalice, and also the chalice itself, unless it is preferred to purify it at the credence table after Mass.

If the priest performs the purification, he says quietly:
“What has passed our lips as food, O Lord, may we possess in purity of heart, that what has been given to us in time may be our healing for eternity.” Then he dries the chalice with the purificator.

If the vessels are purified at the altar, a minister carries them to the credence table. However, it is permitted to leave the vessels to be purified, especially if there are many, on the altar or on the credence table upon a corporal, suitably covered, and to purify them right after Mass, once the people have been dismissed.

After everyone has received Communion, it is fitting to allow a period of silence so that both the priest and the faithful can make the most of these moments of intimacy with the Lord. 

The Holy Father, in his apostolic exhortation Sacramentum Caritatis (No. 50), affirms in this regard: “Nor should the precious time of thanksgiving after Communion be neglected: in addition to a fitting hymn, it can also be very helpful to remain recollected in silence.”

To conclude the supplication of the People of God, and also to bring the entire Communion Rite to a close, the priest says the prayer after Communion, in which the fruits of the mystery celebrated are asked for.

At Mass, only one prayer after Communion is said, and it ends with a short conclusion, namely:

If addressed to the Father: 

`“Through Christ our Lord.”`

If addressed to the Father, but the Son is mentioned at the end: 

`“Who lives and reigns for ever and ever.”`

If addressed to the Son: 

`“Who live and reign for ever and ever.”`

The people make the prayer their own with the acclamation: 

`“Amen.”`

The Concluding Rites include:

a) Brief announcements, if necessary.

b) The greeting and blessing of the priest.

c) The dismissal of the people, given by the [[deacon|Diácono]] or the priest.

d) The kissing of the altar by the priest and the deacon, followed by a profound bow to the altar by the priest, the deacon, and the other ministers.

After the prayer after Communion, the priest greets the people and blesses them, tracing the Sign of the Cross and invoking the Trinity: _"may almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit"_.

What this blessing does is convey, with the efficacy and certainty of the liturgy, a blessing that Christ himself finally grants to his people. Just as the Lord, when taking leave of his disciples at the moment of his Ascension, "lifted up his hands and blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them, and was carried up into heaven" (Lk 24:50-51).

So now, through the priest who represents him, the Lord blesses the Christian people, who have gathered in the Eucharist to celebrate the memorial of _"his saving Passion, his wondrous Resurrection and Ascension into heaven, as we look forward to his second coming"_ (Eucharistic Prayer III).

On certain days and occasions, according to the rubrics, this blessing is enriched and expressed through the prayer over the People or another, more solemn formula.

Finally, the **priest**, with hands joined, dismisses the people with one of the formulas from the Missal (Order of Mass, no. 144):

`"Go forth, the Mass is ended";`

or

`"Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord";`

or

`"Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life";`

or

`"Go in peace."`

The **people** respond:

`"Thanks be to God"`


The word Mass comes from the Latin verb _mittere_, meaning "to send." The celebration of the Eucharist ends with the sending forth of Christians into the world, just as Christ sends his disciples before ascending: _"go into all the world and preach the gospel to the whole creation"_ (Mk 16:15).

![flip:square|50|left|CARD_CUADRADA_ENVIO.jpg~|text|~Christ chooses us and sends us forth.~dark]
Pope Benedict XVI noted that in the words _Ite, missa est_ we can see the relationship between the Mass celebrated and the Christian mission: the term _missa_ is transformed into **mission**. Participation in the Eucharist cannot be reduced to an intimate personal experience; it must impel the faithful to be witnesses of Christ in the world (_Sacramentum Caritatis_).

sections.title: Understand Other Aspects of the Mass

content.text: **The "Strong" Sundays (Advent, Lent, and Easter): ** These have such a high rank in the table of liturgical precedence that they outrank any Solemnity. If a solemnity (such as Saint Joseph or the Annunciation) falls on one of these Sundays, the solemnity must be moved to the following Monday, because the Sunday cannot yield its place.

**Sundays in Ordinary Time and Christmastide:** These have an intermediate rank. They carry more weight than Feasts and Memorials, but yield their place before Solemnities of the Lord, of Our Lady, or of the saints (for example, if the feast of Saints Peter and Paul falls on an ordinary Sunday, the Solemnity is celebrated instead of the usual Sunday Mass).

**Solemnities:** these are the celebrations of the highest rank, reserved for the most important mysteries of our faith — for example, Easter, Pentecost, Christ the King, and so on. They require the Gloria and the Creed.
**Feasts:** Feasts honor some mystery or title of Jesus, of Our Lady, or of particularly important saints. They require the Gloria.
**Memorials:** A memorial is generally the celebration of a saint, but it could also celebrate some aspect of Jesus or Mary. We have obligatory memorials and optional memorials.

**Weekdays (feriae):** This is the name given to the days of the week following Sunday. On these days there is no proper office, nor memorial of any saint. Privileged weekdays include Ash Wednesday and those of Holy Week, and the Advent weekdays from December 17 to 24.
**White:** Feasts of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Blessed Virgin Mary, and saints who were not martyrs. A symbol of glory, joy, innocence, and purity of soul.
**Red:** Pentecost, the Holy Spirit, feasts of the Apostles and martyrs. It signifies the fire of charity and the blood shed by Christ.
**Green:** Ordinary Time of the year. It signifies hope.
**Purple:** Advent and Lent. A sign of humility and penance.
**Black:** May be used, where customary, at Masses for the Dead.
**Rose:** May be used, where customary, on Gaudete Sunday (Third Sunday of Advent) and Laetare Sunday (Fourth Sunday of Lent).

**Sky Blue (purity and virginity):**
This is a privilege of Spain and its former territories, for the solemnity of the Immaculate Conception (Dec. 8), its octave (the eight days following), and Saturdays on which this votive Mass is used.

subsections.title: The Mass Is a Communal Act

content.value:
Liturgical celebrations are, above all, communal acts; they are not private acts.


![img:catholic-church-england-and-wales-008.jpg|right|w:50%]
For this reason, our prayers, gestures, and postures should be carried out in community, with everyone doing them together, as the Magisterium of the Church directs.

There are a number of gestures that do not appear in the Missal and yet many people perform them as though they were normal. On the other hand, there are gestures that are indicated and yet very few people actually make them.

A very clear example is found in the Creed (or _symbolum_): did you know that when we pray the Creed we should make a bow?

_[...] and for our salvation he came down from heaven_

**(At the words that follow, up to and including and became man, all bow)**

_and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. [...]_

Examples of personal devotions that are not indicated in the General Instruction of the Roman Missal:

- Making the Sign of the Cross before the Sign of Peace, and before or after receiving Communion.

- Raising one's hands during “Through him, and with him, and in him...” or during “For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours...” or when we say “And with your spirit.”

- Saying aloud “My Lord and my God” during the Consecration (it is better said interiorly).

content.text:
Mass is not something you “attend to hear” — it is something you take part in.

In the liturgical action there is no room for spectators or passive members; unfortunately, even today we can still hear people say: “I've come to hear Mass.”

As Sacrosanctum Concilium, no. 11, tells us, “the faithful take part fully aware of what they are doing, actively engaged in the rite.”

definitions.definition:
The altar is the table of sacrifice and of banquet at which the priest, representing Christ the Lord, does what he himself did and commanded his disciples to do in his memory.

When Christ the Lord, in instituting the memorial of the sacrifice he was to offer to the Father on the altar of the cross, wished the table around which the faithful would gather to celebrate his Passover, under the form of a sacrificial banquet, to be made holy. Indeed, the altar is the table of sacrifice and of banquet at which the priest, representing Christ the Lord, does what he himself did and commanded his disciples to do in his memory. All this was admirably summed up by the Apostle St. Paul, when he says: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread" (1 Cor 10:16-17).

The ambo is the sacred, reserved liturgical place from which the Word of God alone is proclaimed. Designed as a fixed, elevated structure that manifests the dignity of the divine message, it is considered the "Table of the Word," from which the readings, the Psalm, the Gospel, and the homily are given (the homily may also be given from the chair), connecting directly with the altar, or Table of the Eucharist.

The chalice is the sacred vessel used to consecrate the wine that will become the Blood of Christ at Mass. It must be made of gold, or of silver gilded on the inside, or it may be a silver cup gilded on the inside, in which case the base and stem may be of any solid, clean, and suitable metal (Roman Missal, Ritus celebr., tit. I, n. 1).

The base may be round, hexagonal, or octagonal, and must be large enough that there is no fear of the chalice tipping over. Near the middle of the stem, between the base and the cup, it is recommended that there be a knob, so that the chalice can be handled easily, especially after the consecration, when the priest holds his index finger and thumb joined together.

Before the chalice and paten are used in the Sacrifice of the Mass, they must be blessed by a bishop or priest. Furthermore, if the chalice loses its blessing — which happens, for example, if the cup is broken or pierced, or even if it has had to be sent to be regilded — it must be blessed again before it can be used once more.

Strictly speaking, only priests and deacons are permitted to touch the chalice or the paten, but sacristans and those officially appointed to care for the vestments and sacred vessels are often granted permission to do so.

The ciborium is a vessel shaped like a chalice used to hold the Blessed Sacrament.

Two vessels are used to reserve the Blessed Sacrament: one, called a pyx, is a small round box used to carry the Blessed Sacrament to the sick; and the other, generally called a ciborium, is used to distribute Holy Communion in churches and to reserve consecrated particles in the tabernacle.

The ciborium is blessed by a bishop or by a priest delegated by him, according to the form given in the Roman Ritual. While it contains the sacred species it must be covered with a small white silk veil or a golden cloth, and may only be handled by sacred ministers; when empty and purified it may be touched by all clerics (Congregation of Rites, January 1907), and by specially authorized laypeople.

The corporal is a square white linen cloth spread over the altar during Mass to hold the chalice, the ciborium, and the paten. Its name comes from the Latin *corpus*, meaning Body, since the Body of the Lord rests upon it. It has traditionally been associated with the holy shroud.

Its use at Mass is mandatory (GIRM 80). It must also be used in the exposition of the Blessed Sacrament, to hold the monstrance or ciborium. It is likewise placed on a small table when Communion is brought to the sick.

The corporal is always folded inward in a very specific way (into nine squares) so that, if any particle happened to fall directly onto the cloth, it will not fall to the ground when it is removed. At Mass it is spread on the altar at the moment of the offertory, and after Communion it is folded and put away.

The deacon is the minister who has received the first degree of the Sacrament of Holy Orders. His mission is configured to Christ the Servant, exercising his ministry in the liturgy, the proclamation of the Word, and the works of charity of the Church, in communion with the Bishop and the presbyterate.

Unlike the priest and the bishop, the deacon does not possess the ministerial priesthood nor does he act *in persona Christi Capitis* (in the person of Christ the Head), and so he cannot perform the Eucharistic consecration or grant the forgiveness of sins in Reconciliation. Nevertheless, as an ordinary minister he is empowered to impart blessings, baptize, assist at and bless Marriage, proclaim the Holy Gospel, and preach the homily. Likewise, the diaconate may be permanent and conferred on married men.

Sunday: the Day of the Lord and the primordial feast of the universal Church. Because it commemorates the Resurrection of Christ, it is considered "the weekly Easter" and holds a unique rank: it stands above memorials and feasts, and even the Sundays of Advent, Lent, and Easter carry more weight than any solemnity. On Sunday the singing of the Gloria and the recitation of the Creed are obligatory.

Solemnities: the celebrations of the highest rank, reserved for the most important mysteries of our faith (for example, Easter, Pentecost, Christ the King). On these the singing of the Gloria and the recitation of the Creed are obligatory.

Feasts: these honor some mystery or title of Jesus, of the Virgin Mary, or of saints of particular importance to the universal Church. On these celebrations the Gloria is obligatory, but the Creed is omitted.

Memorials: these are generally the celebrations of the saints, though they can also commemorate some aspect of Jesus or of the Virgin Mary. They are divided into obligatory memorials (which must be celebrated) and free or optional ones (left to the celebrant's discretion).

Weekdays (ferias): this is the name given to days of the week on which none of the above celebrations falls. They have no office of their own and do not commemorate a particular saint. The weekdays of Holy Week, Ash Wednesday, and the weekdays of Advent from December 17 to 24 are exceptionally "privileged."

The Book of the Gospels is the liturgical book that contains exclusively the texts of the four Gospels. It is reserved for Sundays and great feasts, remaining on the altar until the moment of its solemn proclamation.

Because of its special dignity, representing as it does the presence of Christ in his Word, it is the only book that may be carried in the entrance procession by the deacon or the lector, and the only one placed on the altar until the moment of its proclamation at the ambo. It is distinguished from the Lectionary in that it possesses greater artistic and solemn richness, receiving specific honors during the liturgy, such as incensation and the celebrant's kiss at the end of the reading.

When a grave impediment exists, the precept of attending Mass is lifted. In these cases, the Church does not bind you to the impossible. Technically, watching Mass on television or online is not "attending" Mass, since the liturgy requires physical presence and participation in sacramental communion. However, for someone who is gravely impeded, watching it is a most praiseworthy and recommended act of piety that helps to sanctify the Lord's day.

Funeral rites are the set of rites and prayers the Catholic Church celebrates upon the death of one of the faithful. Their principal meaning is to celebrate the paschal mystery (the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ), bidding farewell to the person on behalf of the community and entrusting his or her soul to divine mercy.

The Roman Gradual (Graduale Romanum) is the liturgical book that contains all the parts of the Mass to be sung by the choir or schola cantorum throughout the year (entrance chants, graduals, alleluias, offertory chants, and communion chants). Its texts are set almost entirely to Gregorian chant, using the classic four-line staff notation (tetragram).

There is another version called the Graduale Simplex (Simple Gradual), created after the Second Vatican Council, which offers much simpler and more accessible melodies for parishes that do not have a professional Gregorian chant choir.

The Lectionary is the liturgical book that gathers, in an orderly arrangement, the readings from Sacred Scripture (Old Testament, Psalms, Gospel, and Epistles) assigned for each day of the year. Unlike the Book of the Gospels, the Lectionary remains at the ambo at all times and is used at every celebration, including ordinary weekday Masses. It is divided according to the liturgical cycles (A, B, and C for Sundays; I and II for weekdays) and specific seasons.
The lavabo towel is a cloth with which the celebrant dries his hands when he washes them at Mass. It may be made of linen, of toweling, or of any other absorbent material.

This is the official liturgical book containing the presidential prayers and the rubrics (instructions) needed to celebrate the Eucharist. Its contents are divided into the Order of Mass — the fixed parts of the rite — and the Proper — prayers that vary according to the season or feast. Although it is also used at the chair during the introductory and concluding rites, its principal place is the altar, where the priest uses it to proclaim the Preface and the Eucharistic Prayer, the high point that includes the Consecration.

The Bishop is the ordained minister who possesses the third degree and the fullness of the Sacrament of Holy Orders. As a direct successor of the Apostles, he is the chief shepherd and the highest authority of a diocese, responsible for teaching, sanctifying, and governing the ecclesial community in communion with the Pope.

Unlike the deacon and the priest, the bishop possesses the fullness of apostolic authority, which makes him the only minister capable of conferring the Sacrament of Holy Orders in all its degrees. While priests and deacons exercise their ministry in a delegated way in parishes or local services, the bishop holds ordinary power and pastoral care over the entire particular Church (diocese) entrusted to him.

This is the name given to the body of texts and rites that, being unchanging by nature, are repeated at every Eucharistic celebration, forming the fixed structure of the liturgy (such as the Kyrie, Gloria, Creed, Preface, and doxology). It is distinguished from the "Proper," which comprises the prayers and readings that vary according to the liturgical season or the feast of the saint being celebrated.

The pall is a square piece of stiff cloth, generally of starched white linen, used to cover the chalice during the celebration of Mass, as part of the Eucharistic ritual. Its main purpose is to protect the contents of the chalice and the sacred elements from dust, insects, or other outside contaminants; among these linens, it occupies a place of its own because of its specific use over the sacred vessels.

No rubric requires it, but liturgical manuals recommend that, when placing or removing the pall from the chalice, the left hand be kept on the base of the chalice, so as to avoid accidentally tipping over this sacred vessel. In this way, the left hand rests on the base of the chalice while the right hand handles the pall.

The eucharistic vessel known as the paten is a small, shallow plate or disc of precious metal on which the element of bread is offered to God at the offertory of the Mass, and on which the consecrated host is placed again after the fraction.

The paten must be made of gold or of gilded silver, and may not be used until a bishop has consecrated it with chrism. The formula used speaks of the vessel as blessed "for the administration of the Eucharist of Jesus Christ, that the Body of our Lord may be broken upon it"; and also as "the new sepulcher of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ."

The pyx (from the Latin *pyx*, Gr. *pyxis*) is a small vessel meant to hold the Blessed Sacrament (consecrated Hosts), above all for carrying Viaticum to the sick. Often the communion pyx is worn around the neck. This reminds the person carrying it, as well as those around them, that they are carrying the Blessed Sacrament.

At times a pyx is carried in a small pouch-like bag designed to further protect the pyx and the consecrated hosts inside it. Above all, the pyx must be handled with the utmost care, in recognition that whoever holds it with the Eucharist inside is holding Jesus, the Lord.

This is the principal area where the liturgy takes place, generally set off by steps or a rail to distinguish it from the nave. Here are found the altar; the chair — the seat of the presiding celebrant (priest or bishop); the ambo — the stand from which the Word of God is proclaimed; and the credence table — a small side table used by the ministers.

The priest — commonly known as father — is the minister who has received the second degree of the Sacrament of Holy Orders and collaborates directly with the Bishop in his pastoral mission.

Unlike the deacon, the priest does share in the ministerial priesthood, which enables him to act *in persona Christi Capitis* to consecrate the Eucharist and absolve sins. On the other hand, unlike the bishop, the priest does not possess the fullness of Holy Orders, so his faculties depend on communion with his own Bishop, and he cannot confer the Sacrament of Holy Orders (ordain deacons or priests) or habitually administer Confirmation; he is, moreover, called to lead a specific parish community rather than an entire diocese.

The set of liturgical texts and chants that vary according to the day, the feast, or the liturgical season (Advent, Lent, Easter, Ordinary Time). It comprises the presidential prayers (the Collect, the Prayer over the Offerings, and the Prayer after Communion), the biblical readings from the Lectionary, and the entrance and communion antiphons. Its purpose is to highlight the specific mystery of the life of Christ, or the memory of the saints, that the Church celebrates on a given date.

The purificator is a piece of pure white linen or hemp cloth used to clean the chalice. It is folded into three layers. A small cross may be embroidered at its center to distinguish it from the small finger towels used at the "lavabo," though this is not prescribed. It is not blessed.

Before Mass it is placed over the chalice, and above the purificator the paten is set with the largest host. At the offertory, before the chalice is prepared, it is placed to the right of the corporal, and from there it is taken up for use by the priest. After the ablutions, it is again placed over the chalice, as it was at the start of Mass.

Etymological meaning: the word comes from the Latin *rubrica* (which derives from *ruber*, red). It receives this name because, in printed liturgical books, these instructions have traditionally been written in red letters to distinguish them from the text that the priest or the assembly is to say or sing, which is printed in black letters.

Purpose: the rubrics do not contain the prayers themselves, but the operative instructions. They indicate:

Gestures and bodily postures: when to stand, kneel, sit, bow, extend the hands, or make the sign of the cross.

Ritual actions: when to incense the altar, pour the wine and water into the chalice, wash the hands, or kiss the altar.

Movements and ministries: who is to perform each action (the priest, the deacon, the acolyte, or the lector) and in what part of the sanctuary.

Permitted options: when the celebrant is allowed to choose among different formulas or introductions, depending on pastoral circumstances.

In summary: a classic principle governs liturgical books: "What is black is said (or sung), what is red is done." The rubrics are precisely "the red" — the map of action that guarantees the solemnity, order, and universality of the Mass.

The tabernacle is the space in the church set aside for the reservation of the Eucharist. It is not only a place of safekeeping; it is also a space where the faithful can pray before Jesus.

Until the Second Vatican Council, liturgical norms required that the tabernacle be placed at the very center of the altar.

Today, this has changed.
GIRM 314: "In accordance with the structure of each church and legitimate local customs, the Most Blessed Sacrament should be reserved in a tabernacle in a part of the church that is truly noble, prominent, readily visible, beautifully decorated, and suitable for prayer. The one tabernacle should be immovable, be made of solid and inviolable material that is not transparent, and be locked in such a way that the danger of profanation is prevented to the greatest extent possible. Moreover, it is appropriate that, before it is put into liturgical use, it be blessed according to the rite described in the Roman Ritual."

GIRM 316: "In accordance with traditional custom, near the tabernacle a special lamp, fueled by oil or wax, should be kept alight to indicate and honor the presence of Christ."

The seat of the priest presiding over a liturgical celebration is called the chair. It must be in a fitting place that allows the priest to be seen as the one presiding over the assembly and moderating the prayer. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal indicates that its most suitable place is facing the people, at the head of the sanctuary, unless the structure of the building or some other circumstance prevents this — for example, if the great distance would make communication between the priest and the gathered assembly difficult, or if the tabernacle is located in the middle, behind the altar (n. 310).

In the cathedral of each diocese, instead of a chair there is a cathedra, a sign of the teaching authority and power of the pastor of the particular Church, and a sign of the unity of the believers in the faith the bishop proclaims as shepherd of his flock.

Only the diocesan bishop may sit in the cathedra, though he may permit another bishop to sit in it (Ceremonial of Bishops, nn. 47 and 174). If a bishop celebrates in a cathedral that is not his own, or a priest celebrates in the cathedral, he must sit in a seat other than the cathedra, which must be prepared for him for that purpose.

Ordinary Time is the longest liturgical season of the year (made up of 33 or 34 weeks) and is divided into two periods: the first falls between Christmas and Lent, and the second between Pentecost and Advent. Far from meaning something "common" or of lesser importance, the word ordinary comes from "order," pointing to the Church's ordered, progressive journey. During these weeks the liturgical color is green, and no single mystery of the life of Jesus is celebrated; instead, his public life, his miracles, and his teachings are contemplated in their entirety.

Decree on the Eucharist of the Council of Trent: "Because Christ our Redeemer said that it was truly his body that he was offering under the species of bread, it has always been the conviction of the Church of God, and this holy Council now declares it anew, that by the consecration of the bread and wine there takes place a change of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord, and of the whole substance of the wine into the substance of his blood. This change the holy Catholic Church has fittingly and properly named transubstantiation" (Council of Trent (1551): DS 1642, cited in CCC 1376).

Transubstantiation, a change of substance. The substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ himself (body, blood, soul, and divinity), although the bread and wine retain their properties, or accidents.

A small vessel for holding the wine and water needed for the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass. Two are always used. The Roman Missal (Rubricae Gen., XX) prescribes that they be made of glass. This is the most suitable material because it is easily cleaned, and its transparency avoids any danger of confusing the water and the wine. However, other materials are also used, such as gold, silver, and other precious metals. In that case it is advisable to mark the wine cruet with a V (Vinum) and the water cruet with an A (Aqua), so that they can be told apart easily.

Before Mass, they should be placed on the credence table with enough water and wine. From there they are brought to the altar to prepare the chalice. Afterward, they are returned to the credence table. If the faithful present the wine to the priest at the offertory, they are placed on a table outside the sanctuary, where the faithful take them from. Once the chalice has been prepared, they are brought back to the credence table.

paragraphs.text: When he was about to celebrate with his disciples the Passover meal in which he instituted the sacrifice of his Body and Blood, Christ the Lord gave instructions that a large, furnished upper room should be prepared (Lk 22:12). The Church has always regarded this command as applying also to herself when she gives directions about the preparation of people’s hearts and minds and of the places, rites, and texts for the celebration of the Most Holy Eucharist. The current norms, prescribed in keeping with the will of the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, and the new Missal that the Church of the Roman Rite is to use from now on in the celebration of Mass are also evidence of the great concern of the Church, of her faith, and of her unchanged love for the great mystery of the Eucharist. They likewise bear witness to the Church’s continuous and unbroken tradition, irrespective of the introduction of certain new features. A Witness to Unchanged Faith

The sacrificial nature of the Mass, solemnly asserted by the Council of Trent in accordance with the Church’s universal tradition,[1] was reaffirmed by the Second Vatican Council, which offered these significant words about the Mass: “At the Last Supper our Savior instituted the Eucharistic Sacrifice of his Body and Blood, by which he would perpetuate the Sacrifice of the Cross throughout the centuries until he should come again, thus entrusting to the Church, his beloved Bride, the memorial of his death and resurrection.”[2] What the Council thus teaches is expressed constantly in the formulas of the Mass. This teaching, which is concisely expressed in the statement already contained in the ancient Sacramentary commonly known as the Leonine—“As often as the commemoration of this sacrifice is celebrated, the work of our redemption is carried out”[3]—is aptly and accurately developed in the Eucharistic Prayers. For in these prayers the priest, while he performs the commemoration, turns towards God, even in the name of the whole people, renders him thanks and offers the living and holy Sacrifice, namely, the Church’s offering and the Victim by whose immolation God willed to be appeased;[4] and he prays that the Body and Blood of Christ may be a sacrifice acceptable to the Father and salvific for the whole world.[5] In this new Missal, then, the Church’s rule of prayer (lex orandi) corresponds to her perennial rule of belief (lex credendi), by which namely we are taught that the Sacrifice of the Cross and its sacramental renewal in the Mass, which Christ the Lord instituted at the Last Supper and commanded the Apostles to do in his memory, are one and the same, differing only in the manner of offering, and that consequently the Mass is at once a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving, of propitiation and satisfaction.

Moreover, the wondrous mystery of the Lord’s real presence under the Eucharistic species, reaffirmed by the Second Vatican Council[6] and other documents of the Church’s Magisterium[7] in the same sense and with the same words that the Council of Trent had proposed as a matter of faith,[8] is proclaimed in the celebration of Mass not only by means of the very words of consecration, by which Christ becomes present through transubstantiation, but also by that interior disposition and outward expression of supreme reverence and adoration in which the Eucharistic Liturgy is carried out. For the same reason the Christian people is drawn on Holy Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, and on the solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, to venerate this wonderful Sacrament by a special form of adoration.

Further, the nature of the ministerial priesthood proper to a Bishop and a priest, who offer the Sacrifice in the person of Christ and who preside over the gathering of the holy people, is evident in the form of the rite itself, by reason of the more prominent place and office of the priest. The meaning of this office is enunciated and explained clearly and at greater length in the Preface for the Chrism Mass on Holy Thursday, the day commemorating the institution of the priesthood. The Preface brings to light the conferral of the priestly power accomplished through the laying on of hands; and, by listing the various duties, it describes that power, which is the continuation of the power of Christ the High Priest of the New Testament.

In addition, the nature of the ministerial priesthood also puts into its proper light another reality, which must indeed be highly regarded, namely, the royal priesthood of the faithful, whose spiritual sacrifice is brought to completeness through the ministry of the Bishop and the priests in union with the sacrifice of Christ, the one and only Mediator.[9] For the celebration of the Eucharist is an action of the whole Church, and in it each one should carry out solely but completely that which pertains to him or her, in virtue of the rank of each within the People of God. In this way greater consideration will also be given to some aspects of the celebration that have sometimes been accorded less attention in the course of time. For this people is the People of God, purchased by Christ’s Blood, gathered together by the Lord, nourished by his word. It is a people called to bring to God the prayers of the entire human family, a people giving thanks in Christ for the mystery of salvation by offering his Sacrifice. Finally, it is a people made one by sharing in the Communion of Christ’s Body and Blood. Though holy in its origin, this people nevertheless grows continually in holiness by its conscious, active, and fruitful participation in the mystery of the Eucharist.[10] A Witness to Unbroken Tradition

In setting forth its instructions for the revision of the Order of Mass, the Second Vatican Council, using the same words as did St. Pius V in the Apostolic Constitution Quo primum, by which the Missal of Trent was promulgated in 1570, also ordered, among other things, that some rites be restored “to the original norm of the holy Fathers.”[11] From the fact that the same words are used it can be seen how both Roman Missals, although separated by four centuries, embrace one and the same tradition. Furthermore, if the inner elements of this tradition are reflected upon, it also becomes clear how outstandingly and felicitously the older Roman Missal is brought to fulfillment in the new.

In a difficult period when the Catholic faith on the sacrificial nature of the Mass, the ministerial priesthood, and the real and permanent presence of Christ under the Eucharistic species were placed at risk, St. Pius V was especially concerned with preserving the more recent tradition, then unjustly being assailed, introducing only very slight changes into the sacred rite. In fact, the Missal of 1570 differs very little from the very first printed edition of 1474, which in turn faithfully follows the Missal used at the time of Pope Innocent III. Moreover, even though manuscripts in the Vatican Library provided material for the emendation of some expressions, they by no means made it possible to inquire into “ancient and approved authors” farther back than the liturgical commentaries of the Middle Ages.

Today, on the other hand, countless learned studies have shed light on the “norm of the holy Fathers” which the revisers of the Missal of St. Pius V followed. For following the publication first of the Sacramentary known as the Gregorian in 1571, critical editions of other ancient Roman and Ambrosian Sacramentaries were published, often in book form, as were ancient Hispanic and Gallican liturgical books which brought to light numerous prayers of no slight spiritual excellence that had previously been unknown. In a similar fashion, traditions dating back to the first centuries, before the formation of the rites of East and West, are better known today because of the discovery of so many liturgical documents. Moreover, continuing progress in the study of the holy Fathers has also shed light upon the theology of the mystery of the Eucharist through the teachings of such illustrious Fathers of Christian antiquity as St. Irenaeus, St. Ambrose, St. Cyril of Jerusalem, and St. John Chrysostom.

For this reason, the “norm of the holy Fathers” requires not only the preservation of what our immediate forebears have passed on to us, but also an understanding and a more profound study of the Church’s entire past and of all the ways in which her one and only faith has been set forth in the quite diverse human and social forms prevailing in the Semitic, Greek, and Latin areas. Moreover, this broader view allows us to see how the Holy Spirit endows the People of God with a marvelous fidelity in preserving the unalterable deposit of faith, even amid a very great variety of prayers and rites. Accommodation to New Conditions

The new Missal, therefore, while bearing witness to the Roman Church’s rule of prayer (lex orandi), also safeguards the deposit of faith handed down by the more recent Councils and marks in its own right a step of great importance in liturgical tradition. Indeed, when the Fathers of the Second Vatican Council reaffirmed the dogmatic pronouncements of the Council of Trent, they spoke at a far different time in world history, so that they were able to bring forward proposals and measures of a pastoral nature that could not have even been foreseen four centuries earlier.

The Council of Trent already recognized the great catechetical value contained in the celebration of Mass but was unable to bring out all its consequences in regard to actual practice. In fact, many were pressing for permission to use the vernacular in celebrating the Eucharistic Sacrifice; but the Council, weighing the conditions of that age, considered it a duty to answer this request with a reaffirmation of the Church’s traditional teaching, according to which the Eucharistic Sacrifice is, first and foremost, the action of Christ himself, and therefore its proper efficacy is unaffected by the manner in which the faithful take part in it. The Council for this reason stated in firm but measured words, “Although the Mass contains much instruction for people of faith, nevertheless it did not seem expedient to the Fathers that it be celebrated everywhere in the vernacular.”[12] The Council accordingly anathematized anyone maintaining that “the rite of the Roman Church, in which part of the Canon and the words of consecration are spoken in a low voice, is to be condemned, or that the Mass must be celebrated only in the vernacular.”[13] Although on the one hand it prohibited the use of the vernacular in the Mass, nevertheless, on the other hand, the Council did direct pastors of souls to put appropriate catechesis in its place: “Lest Christ’s flock go hungry . . . the Holy Synod commands pastors and all others having the care of souls to give frequent instructions during the celebration of Mass, either personally or through others, concerning what is read at Mass; among other things, they should include some explanation of the mystery of this most holy Sacrifice, especially on Sundays and holy days.”[14]

Therefore, when the Second Vatican Council convened in order to accommodate the Church to the requirements of her proper apostolic office precisely in these times, it examined thoroughly, as had Trent, the instructive and pastoral character of the sacred Liturgy.[15] Since no Catholic would now deny the lawfulness and efficacy of a sacred rite celebrated in Latin, the Council was also able to grant that “the use of the vernacular language may frequently be of great advantage to the people” and gave the faculty for its use.1[16] The enthusiasm in response to this measure has been so great everywhere that it has led, under the leadership of the Bishops and the Apostolic See itself, to permission for all liturgical celebrations in which the people participate to be in the vernacular, for the sake of a better comprehension of the mystery being celebrated.

Indeed, since the use of the vernacular in the sacred Liturgy may certainly be considered an important means for presenting more clearly the catechesis regarding the mystery that is inherent in the celebration itself, the Second Vatican Council also ordered that certain prescriptions of the Council of Trent that had not been followed everywhere be brought to fruition, such as the homily to be given on Sundays and holy days[17] and the faculty to interject certain explanations during the sacred rites themselves.[18] Above all, the Second Vatican Council, which urged “that more perfect form of participation in the Mass by which the faithful, after the priest’s Communion, receive the Lord’s Body from the same Sacrifice,”[19] called for another desire of the Fathers of Trent to be realized, namely that for the sake of a fuller participation in the holy Eucharist “the faithful present at each Mass should communicate not only by spiritual desire but also by sacramental reception of the Eucharist.”[20]

Moved by the same desire and pastoral concern, the Second Vatican Council was able to give renewed consideration to what was established by Trent on Communion under both kinds. And indeed, since no one today calls into doubt in any way the doctrinal principles on the complete efficacy of Eucharistic Communion under the species of bread alone, the Council thus gave permission for the reception of Communion under both kinds on some occasions, because this clearer form of the sacramental sign offers a particular opportunity of deepening the understanding of the mystery in which the faithful take part.[21]

In this manner the Church, while remaining faithful to her office as teacher of truth safeguarding “things old,” that is, the deposit of tradition, fulfills at the same time another duty, that of examining and prudently bringing forth “things new” (cf. Mt 13:52). Accordingly, a part of the new Missal directs the prayers of the Church in a more open way to the needs of our times, which is above all true of the Ritual Masses and the Masses for Various Needs, in which tradition and new elements are appropriately harmonized. Thus, while many expressions, drawn from the Church’s most ancient tradition and familiar through the many editions of The Roman Missal, have remained unchanged, many other expressions have been accommodated to today’s needs and circumstances. Still others, such as the prayers for the Church, the laity, the sanctification of human work, the community of all peoples, and certain needs proper to our era, have been newly composed, drawing on the thoughts and often the very phrasing of the recent documents of the Council. Moreover, on account of the same attitude toward the new state of the present world, it seemed that in the use of texts from the most ancient tradition, so revered a treasure would in no way be harmed if some phrases were changed so that the style of language would be more in accord with the language of modern theology and would truly reflect the current discipline of the Church. Thus, not a few expressions bearing on the evaluation and use of the goods of the earth have been changed, as have also not a few allusions to a certain form of outward penance belonging to past ages of the Church. Finally, in this manner the liturgical norms of the Council of Trent have certainly been completed and perfected in many respects by those of the Second Vatican Council, which has brought to realization the efforts of the last four hundred years to bring the faithful closer to the sacred Liturgy especially in recent times, and above all the zeal for the Liturgy promoted by St. Pius X and his successors.

The celebration of Mass, as the action of Christ and the People of God arrayed hierarchically, is the center of the whole Christian life for the Church both universal and local, as well as for each of the faithful individually.[22] In it is found the high point both of the action by which God sanctifies the world in Christ and of the worship that the human race offers to the Father, adoring him through Christ, the Son of God, in the Holy Spirit.[23] In it, moreover, during the course of the year, the mysteries of redemption are recalled so as in some way to be made present.[24] Furthermore, the other sacred actions and all the activities of the Christian life are bound up with it, flow from it, and are ordered to it.[25]

It is therefore of the greatest importance that the celebration of the Mass—that is, the Lord’s Supper—be so arranged that the sacred ministers and the faithful taking part in it, according to the proper state of each, may derive from it more abundantly[26] those fruits for the sake of which Christ the Lord instituted the Eucharistic Sacrifice of his Body and Blood and entrusted it to the Church, his beloved Bride, as the memorial of his Passion and Resurrection.[27]

This will best be accomplished if, with due regard for the nature and the particular circumstances of each liturgical assembly, the entire celebration is planned in such a way that it leads to a conscious, active, and full participation of the faithful both in body and in mind, a participation burning with faith, hope, and charity, of the sort which is desired by the Church and demanded by the very nature of the celebration, and to which the Christian people have a right and duty by reason of their Baptism.[28]

Even if it is sometimes not possible to have the presence and active participation of the faithful, which bring out more plainly the ecclesial nature of the celebration,[29] the Eucharistic Celebration always retains its efficacy and dignity because it is the action of Christ and the Church, in which the priest fulfills his own principal office and always acts for the people’s salvation. It is therefore recommended that the priest celebrate the Eucharistic Sacrifice even daily, if possible.[30]

Because, however, the celebration of the Eucharist, like the entire Liturgy, is carried out through perceptible signs that nourish, strengthen, and express faith,[31] the utmost care must be taken to choose and to arrange those forms and elements set forth by the Church that, in view of the circumstances of the people and the place, will more effectively foster active and full participation and more properly respond to the spiritual needs of the faithful.
This Instruction aims both to offer general guidelines for properly arranging the Celebration of the Eucharist and to set forth rules for ordering the various forms of celebration.[32]

The celebration of the Eucharist in a particular Church is of utmost importance. For the diocesan Bishop, the chief steward of the mysteries of God in the particular Church entrusted to his care, is the moderator, promoter, and guardian of the whole of its liturgical life.[33] In celebrations at which the Bishop presides, and especially in the celebration of the Eucharist led by the Bishop himself with the presbyterate, the deacons, and the people taking part, the mystery of the Church is revealed. For this reason, the solemn celebration of Masses of this sort must be an example for the entire diocese. The Bishop should therefore be determined that the priests, the deacons, and the lay Christian faithful grasp ever more deeply the genuine meaning of the rites and liturgical texts, and thereby be led to an active and fruitful celebration of the Eucharist. To the same end, he should also be vigilant that the dignity of these celebrations be enhanced. In promoting this dignity, the beauty of the sacred place, of music, and of art should contribute as greatly as possible.

Moreover, in order that such a celebration may correspond more fully to the prescriptions and spirit of the sacred Liturgy, and also in order to increase its pastoral effectiveness, certain accommodations and adaptations are specified in this General Instruction and in the Order of Mass.

These adaptations consist for the most part in the choice of certain rites or texts, that is, of the chants, readings, prayers, explanations, and gestures which may respond better to the needs, preparation, and culture of the participants and which are entrusted to the priest celebrant., the priest must remember that he is the servant of the sacred Liturgy and that he himself is not permitted, on his own initiative, to add, to remove, or to change anything in the celebration of Mass.[34]

In addition, certain adaptations are indicated in the proper place in the Missal and pertain respectively to the diocesan Bishop or to the Conference of Bishops, in accord with the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy[35] (cf. nos. 387, 388-393).

As for variations and the more substantial adaptations in view of the traditions and culture of peoples and regions, to be introduced in accordance with article 40 of the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy because of benefit or need, the norms set forth in the Instruction On the Roman Liturgy and Inculturation[36] and in nos. 395-399 are to be observed.

At Mass—that is, the Lord’s Supper—the People of God is called together, with a priest presiding and acting in the person of Christ, to celebrate the memorial of the Lord, the Eucharistic Sacrifice.[37] For this reason Christ’s promise applies in an outstanding way to such a local gathering of the holy Church: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Mt 18:20). For in the celebration of Mass, in which the Sacrifice of the Cross is perpetuated,[38] Christ is really present in the very liturgical assembly gathered in his name, in the person of the minister, in his word, and indeed substantially and continuously under the Eucharistic species.[39]

The Mass is made up, as it were, of two parts: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist. These, however, are so closely interconnected that they form but one single act of worship.[40] For in the Mass the table both of God’s word and of Christ’s Body is prepared, from which the faithful may be instructed and refreshed.[41] There are also certain rites that open and conclude the celebration. Reading and Explaining the Word of God

When the Sacred Scriptures are read in the Church, God himself speaks to his people, and Christ, present in his own word, proclaims the Gospel. Therefore, all must listen with reverence to the readings from God’s word, for they make up an element of greatest importance in the Liturgy. Although in the readings from Sacred Scripture God’s word is addressed to all people of every era and is understandable to them, nevertheless, a fuller understanding and a greater effectiveness of the word is fostered by a living commentary on the word, that is, the homily, as part of the liturgical action.[42] The Prayers and Other Parts Pertaining to the Priest

Among the parts assigned to the priest, the foremost is the Eucharistic Prayer, which is the high point of the entire celebration. Next are the orations: that is to say, the collect, the prayer over the offerings, and the prayer after Communion. These prayers are addressed to God in the name of the entire holy people and all present, by the priest who presides over the assembly in the person of Christ.[43] It is with good reason, therefore, that they are called the “presidential prayers.”

It is also up to the priest, in the exercise of his office of presiding over the gathered assembly, to offer certain explanations that are foreseen in the rite itself. Where it is indicated in the rubrics, the celebrant is permitted to adapt them somewhat in order that they respond to the understanding of those participating. However, he should always take care to keep to the sense of the text given in the Missal and to express it succinctly. The presiding priest is also to direct the word of God and to impart the final blessing. In addition, he may give the faithful a very brief introduction to the Mass of the day (after the initial Greeting and before the Act of Penitence), to the Liturgy of the Word (before the readings), and to the Eucharistic Prayer (before the Preface), though never during the Eucharistic Prayer itself; he may also make concluding comments to the entire sacred action before the dismissal.

The nature of the “presidential” texts demands that they be spoken in a loud and clear voice and that everyone listen with attention.[44] Thus, while the priest is speaking these texts, there should be no other prayers or singing, and the organ or other musical instruments should be silent.

The priest, in fact, as the one who presides, prays in the name of the Church and of the assembled community; but at times he prays only in his own name, asking that he may exercise his ministry with greater attention and devotion. Prayers of this kind, which occur before the reading of the Gospel, at the Preparation of the Gifts, and also before and after the Communion of the priest, are said quietly. The Other Formulas in the Celebration

Since the celebration of Mass by its nature has a “communitarian” character,[45] both the dialogues between the priest and the faithful gathered together, and the acclamations are of great significance;[46] in fact, they are not simply outward signs of communal celebration but foster and bring about communion between priest and people.

The acclamations and the responses of the faithful to the priest’s greetings and prayers constitute that level of active participation that the gathered faithful are to contribute in every form of the Mass, so that the action of the entire community may be clearly expressed and fostered.[47]

Other parts, very useful for expressing and fostering the faithful’s active participation, that are assigned to the whole assembly that is called together include especially the Act of Penitence, the Profession of Faith, the Prayer of the Faithful, and the Lord’s Prayer.

Finally, concerning the other formulas: Some constitute an independent rite or act, such as the Gloria, the responsorial Psalm, the Alleluia and verse before the Gospel, the Sanctus, the Memorial Acclamation, and the cantus post communionem (song after communion); Others accompany another rite, such as the chants at the Entrance, at the Offertory, at the fraction (Agnus Dei), and at Communion. The Vocal Expression of the Different Texts

In texts that are to be spoken in a loud and clear voice, whether by the priest or the deacon, or by the lector, or by all, the tone of voice should correspond to the genre of the text itself, that is, depending upon whether it is a reading, a prayer, a commentary, an acclamation, or a sung text; the tone should also be suited to the form of celebration and to the solemnity of the gathering. Consideration should also be given to the idiom of different languages and the culture of different peoples. In the rubrics and in the norms that follow, words such as “say” and “proclaim” are to be understood of both singing and reciting, according to the principles just stated above. The Importance of Singing

The Christian faithful who gather together as one to await the Lord’s coming are instructed by the Apostle Paul to sing together psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (cf. Col 3:16). Singing is the sign of the heart’s joy (cf. Acts 2:46). Thus St. Augustine says rightly, “Singing is for one who loves.”[48] There is also the ancient proverb: “One who sings well prays twice.”

Great importance should therefore be attached to the use of singing in the celebration of the Mass, with due consideration for the culture of the people and abilities of each liturgical assembly. Although it is not always necessary (e.g., in weekday Masses) to sing all the texts that are of themselves meant to be sung, every care should be taken that singing by the ministers and the people is not absent in celebrations that occur on Sundays and on holy days of obligation. In the choosing of the parts actually to be sung, however, preference should be given to those that are of greater importance and especially to those to be sung by the priest or the deacon or the lector, with the people responding, or by the priest and people together.[49]

All other things being equal, Gregorian chant holds pride of place because it is proper to the Roman Liturgy. Other types of sacred music, in particular polyphony, are in no way excluded, provided that they correspond to the spirit of the liturgical action and that they foster the participation of all the faithful.[50] Since faithful from different countries come together ever more frequently, it is fitting that they know how to sing together at least some parts of the Ordinary of the Mass in Latin, especially the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, set to the simpler melodies.[51] Movements and Posture

The gestures and posture of the priest, the deacon, and the ministers, as well as those of the people, ought to contribute to making the entire celebration resplendent with beauty and noble simplicity, so that the true and full meaning of the different parts of the celebration is evident and that the participation of all is fostered.[52] Therefore, attention should be paid to what is determined by this General Instruction and the traditional practice of the Roman Rite and to what serves the common spiritual good of the People of God, rather than private inclination or arbitrary choice. A common posture, to be observed by all participants, is a sign of the unity of the members of the Christian community gathered for the sacred Liturgy: it both expresses and fosters the intention and spiritual attitude of the participants.

The faithful should stand from the beginning of the Entrance chant, or while the priest approaches the altar, until the end of the collect; for the Alleluia chant before the Gospel; while the Gospel itself is proclaimed; during the Profession of Faith and the Prayer of the Faithful; from the invitation, Orate, fratres (Pray, brethren), before the prayer over the offerings until the end of Mass, except at the places indicated below. They should, however, sit while the readings before the Gospel and the responsorial Psalm are proclaimed and for the homily and while the Preparation of the Gifts at the Offertory is taking place; and, as circumstances allow, they may sit or kneel while the period of sacred silence after Communion is observed. In the dioceses of the United States of America, they should kneel beginning after the singing or recitation of the Sanctus until after the Amen of the Eucharistic Prayer, except when prevented on occasion by reasons of health, lack of space, the large number of people present, or some other good reason. Those who do not kneel ought to make a profound bow when the priest genuflects after the consecration. The faithful kneel after the Agnus Dei unless the diocesan Bishop determines otherwise.[53] With a view to a uniformity in gestures and postures during one and the same celebration, the faithful should follow the directions which the deacon, lay minister, or priest gives according to whatever is indicated in the Missal.

Among gestures included are also actions and processions: of the priest going with the deacon and ministers to the altar; of the deacon carrying the Evangeliary or Book of the Gospels to the ambo before the proclamation of the Gospel; of the faithful presenting the gifts and coming forward to receive Communion. It is appropriate that actions and processions of this sort be carried out with decorum while the chants proper to them occur, in keeping with the norms prescribed for each. Silence

Sacred silence also, as part of the celebration, is to be observed at the designated times.[54] Its purpose, however, depends on the time it occurs in each part of the celebration. Thus within the Act of Penitence and again after the invitation to pray, all recollect themselves; but at the conclusion of a reading or the homily, all meditate briefly on what they have heard; then after Communion, they praise and pray to God in their hearts. Even before the celebration itself, it is commendable that silence to be observed in the church, in the sacristy, in the vesting room, and in adjacent areas, so that all may dispose themselves to carry out the sacred action in a devout and fitting manner. A. The Introductory Rites

The rites preceding the Liturgy of the Word, namely the Entrance, Greeting, Act of Penitence, Kyrie, Gloria, and collect, have the character of a beginning, introduction, and preparation. Their purpose is to ensure that the faithful who come together as one establish communion and dispose themselves to listen properly to God’s word and to celebrate the Eucharist worthily. In certain celebrations that are combined with Mass according to the norms of the liturgical books, the Introductory Rites are omitted or performed in a particular way. The Entrance

After the people have gathered, the Entrance chant begins as the priest enters with the deacon and ministers. The purpose of this chant is to open the celebration, foster the unity of those who have been gathered, introduce their thoughts to the mystery of the liturgical season or festivity, and accompany the procession of the priest and ministers.

The singing at this time is done either alternately by the choir and the people or in a similar way by the cantor and the people, or entirely by the people, or by the choir alone. In the dioceses of the United States of America there are four options for the Entrance Chant: (1) the antiphon from The Roman Missal or the Psalm from the Roman Gradual as set to music there or in another musical setting; (2) the seasonal antiphon and Psalm of the Simple Gradual; (3) a song from another collection of psalms and antiphons, approved by the Conference of Bishops or the diocesan Bishop, including psalms arranged in responsorial or metrical forms; (4) a suitable liturgical song similarly approved by the Conference of Bishops or the diocesan Bishop.[55] If there is no singing at the entrance, the antiphon in the Missal is recited either by the faithful, or by some of them, or by a lector; otherwise, it is recited by the priest himself, who may even adapt it as an introductory explanation (cf. no. 31). Greeting of the Altar and of the People Gathered Together

When they reach the sanctuary, the priest, the deacon, and the ministers reverence the altar with a profound bow. As an expression of veneration, moreover, the priest and deacon then kiss the altar itself; as the occasion suggests, the priest also incenses the cross and the altar.

When the Entrance chant is concluded, the priest stands at the chair and, together with the whole gathering, makes the Sign of the Cross. Then he signifies the presence of the Lord to the community gathered there by means of the Greeting. By this Greeting and the people’s response, the mystery of the Church gathered together is made manifest. After the greeting of the people, the priest, the deacon, or a lay minister may very briefly introduce the faithful to the Mass of the day. The Act of Penitence

Then the priest invites those present to take part in the Act of Penitence, which, after a brief pause for silence, the entire community carries out through a formula of general confession. The rite concludes with the priest’s absolution, which, however, lacks the efficacy of the Sacrament of Penance. On Sundays, especially in the Season of Easter, in place of the customary Act of Penitence, from time to time the blessing and sprinkling of water to recall Baptism may take place.[56] The Kyrie Eleison
